# Servius the Grammarian’s Commentary on the Bucolics of Maro <note>Maro refers to Publius Vergilius Maro, known in English as Virgil.</note>

<margin>On the origin of the Bucolic song</margin>
**B**ucolics, as they say, are named from the tending of cattle <note>original: "a custodia boum"</note>; for cattle are the most important animals among country folk. Others, however, provide different reasons for this name.

<margin>Xerxes</margin>
For some say that at the time when Xerxes, the King of the Persians, invaded Greece, when everyone was hiding behind walls and the sacred rites of Diana could not be performed in the usual manner, country folk came to the mountains of Laconia and sang hymns in her honor. They believe the Bucolic poem originated from this event.

<margin>Diana</margin>
<margin>Honorably</margin>
<margin>Scythia</margin>
Others say that when Orestes carried away the statue of Diana Fascelis <note>A title for Diana associated with bundles of sticks or "fasces"</note> stolen from Scythia and was driven to Sicily by a storm, he celebrated the festival of Diana at the completion of a year. Many people were gathered, including some honored shepherds, and from that time the custom remained among the country people.

<margin>Apollo</margin>
<margin>Admetus</margin>
<margin>Opinion</margin>
Others wish this poem to be preserved not for Diana, but for the name of Apollo, from the time when he pastured the herds of King Admetus.

<margin>Pan</margin>
<margin>Satyrs</margin>
Others assert that this song was dedicated by shepherds to the rural deities, to Pan, the nymphs, and the satyrs. And this is the title of this work. Its quality, however, is of the humble style; for there are three "characters" <note>or styles</note> of writing: the humble, the middle, and the grandiloquent.

<margin>Three characters</margin>
All of these are found in this one poet. For in the *Aeneid* he has the grandiloquent style; in the *Georgics*, the middle; and in the *Bucolics*, the humble, according to the quality of the subject matter and the characters. For the characters here are rural folk, rejoicing in simplicity, from whom nothing lofty should be required. Furthermore, regarding the meter of the Bucolics, the fourth foot should end with a part of speech that is a dactyl in itself; for this makes a better verse, such as: "we [leave] the borders of our fatherland" <note>original: "nos patriae fines," quoting the first line of Virgil's Eclogues</note>.

<summary>This page introduces Servius's commentary on Virgil's Bucolics, exploring various mythological origins for the genre and defining its "humble" literary style compared to Virgil's other works.</summary>
<keywords>Servius, Virgil, Bucolics, Eclogues, literary theory, three styles, Diana, Apollo, Xerxes, pastoral poetry</keywords>

This work is well-written in an allegorical style <note>original: "allegorice scriptus"; referring to the hidden political meanings in Virgil's poetry</note>.
At the top <unclear>force</unclear> the fleeces had been. Afterwards, he was sent a formal notice by Augustus, and the entire field <margin>Tritinier <note>Possibly a local place name or a corruption of a legal term regarding land distribution.</note></margin> was restored, as well as a portion of Mantua.
It is for this reason that we read in the first "forest" <note>original: "sylva"; a term often used for a collection of shorter poems</note> of the Eclogues that he described the struggle. Later, we find him complaining as he had heard, and there was a rumor, but the robbery was such that good weapons are of no avail amidst arms. They say the eagle carried off four doves <note>A metaphorical reference to the confiscation of lands by the Roman military</note>.
Neither the number nor the order of the books is in doubt here. Indeed, every book is well-constructed. Regarding the Eclogues, many have doubts, although there are ten of them. It has been discovered, however, in what order they were written. For most of them, he wanted two to be certain, yet so that the neighboring one might be supported by testimony. This title is found in the *Georgics*: "You, reclining under the canopy of a spreading beech" <note>original: "tu patule recumbans sub tegmine fagi"; the famous opening line of Virgil's first Eclogue, quoted here to show how Virgil cross-references his own work</note>. He intended that first one to be the "feather" of fixed things and deigned to play with verse.
Truly, it should be known that seven Eclogues are purely rustic, which Theocritus <note>The Greek poet who invented the pastoral genre</note> also has; in three of them, they take from the rustic style, but in the execution, he departed from it, as in the birthday poem <term>genethliaco <note>A poem written to celebrate a birth, specifically referring here to the 4th "Messianic" Eclogue</note></term> of Solomon <note>The commentator here curiously links Virgil's 4th Eclogue to Solomon, reflecting a medieval Christian interpretation of Virgil as a prophet</note> and in the "forests" of theology, so that he might be able to please others by mixing the works, or because you cannot fill so much with variety.
Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian and Virgil commentator</note> will refute the explanation of the vices in the outcome in the following works.
Truly, it should be known that the good Virgil wrote the *Bucolics* <note>Another name for the Eclogues</note> at twenty-eight years of age; he himself, being bold at the end of the *Georgics*, says that in his youth: "Then you, reclining under the canopy of a spreading beech."
And Donatus says (which we may also see in the name of the poet) that both [aspects] of writing poems are natural.

# An Orderly Examination of the Titles of Virgil

First, his life was pastoral in the mountains; afterward came the love of agriculture; then the care of wars succeeded <note>This refers to the traditional progression of Virgil's works: the Eclogues (pastoral), the Georgics (farming), and the Aeneid (warfare)</note>. It should also be noted that among the Greeks, titles like *Bucolica* or *Georgica* have a specific grammatical article at the end, which we handle differently in our own usage. For it is rare that the final syllable is joyful or that the penultimate is limited in its meter. Furthermore, it must be known that the names of the characters in this work are for the most part derived from rustic origins. For example, Meliboeus is so named because he "seeks the good" <note>original: "Melibeus q̄r euod/ q̄rit bonū"</note> from Tityrus. In the language of the Laconians <note>Spartans</note>, a *tityrus* is what they call a leading ram, who is accustomed to go before the flock. We find similar patterns in pleasant stories: for *Pamphilus* is "all-loving," *Glycerium* is like a "sweet woman," and *Philomela* is "one who loves song." The characters mentioned above are rustic and rejoice in simplicity; hence we find nothing in them that is sophisticated or oratorical. Instead, all their affairs, comparisons, and whatever else exists are drawn from country life. This is why he reckons the years by the harvests, as in: "afterward, seeing my kingdom, I shall marvel at the ears of grain" <note>A reference to Eclogue 1.69</note>. From this also come those comparisons: "For neither does the whistling of the coming south wind delight me so much, nor the shores struck by the fluctuating wave, nor the valleys among the rocky mountains" <note>A paraphrase of Eclogue 5.82-84</note>.

---

->Tityrus, you, reclining under the canopy of a spreading beech tree<- <note>The famous opening line of Virgil's first Eclogue</note>

A certain shepherd is introduced, lying under a fruitful tree and at leisure, giving his attention to song. Another character, however, is shown being driven out from his own borders, while he finds Tityrus at rest. Thus the interpretation follows: and in this place, we ought to understand Tityrus as representing the persona of Virgil himself.

# Commentary on Virgil

In that time, mountains were everywhere / that is, in every place and time where
and before, under the beech tree, he speaks or alleges with fervor
it is most honored, as if under the authority
of the acorn-bearing tree, which was the most ancient.
For in the past, men used to feed upon acorns.

In the fields then, your retained possessions
by which they were nourished, just as they were nourished by acorns.

->Rome composes what is to be celebrated by all nations<-

More than this, and above Meliboeus, Scylla is always such that Tityrus <note>Tityrus and Meliboeus are the two primary shepherds in Virgil's first Eclogue; Tityrus is often seen as a stand-in for the poet himself.</note> sings of his own loves. Meliboeus should understand what god he imitated in Caesar Octavian. **Allegorically**, he is known to have attached this sentiment: *He shall always be a god to me* <note>original: "erit ille michi semper deus" - a famous line from Virgil's Eclogues 1.7.</note>. At this hour, it was necessary to give a color of flattery. *Always*—meaning both after death and while he lives. Others say that emperors are enrolled into the number of the gods after death.

<margin>
Horace.
</margin>
Augustus, for this reason, they purchase temples. Horace says: *To you, while present, we bestow timely honors, and we set up altars to be sworn by in your name.* <note>original: "presenti tibi maturos largim' honores..." - quoting Horace, Epistles 2.1.15-16.</note> Why Tityrus? Concerning Tityrus, but—

<margin>
Lucan.
</margin>
—moved in turn. **Allegorically**, we were Octavian.

<margin>
Ennius.
</margin>
Caesar; at last. Often the Muse is led by all to act blindly. *To imbue* <note>original: "Inbue"</note> is properly to begin and to imitate. No one, however, often begins a good thing at last, but <unclear>as if</unclear> shepherds are often to imitate the pastures, just as we read in the *Georgics*: *Nor through long stretches into the deserts without any guests...* <note>original: "Neqz per longa in deserta..." - referencing Virgil's Georgics.</note> so much is seized as one, whence it is just that shepherds holding the altars find "imbue"; the personae are changed. They find even among the more ancient writers that *to imbue* is not to begin, but to complete and to finish one's own work, because the sense is absolute, as if you were often to pour forth.

*To wander* means to graze as he wishes, as my [flock] favors; and they wander in the mountains, that is, to play or to write songs. *I who played at being a shepherd* <note>original: "qui lusi pastoru'"</note>. Horace says: *I am able, if anything under the idle shade I have played, held by a rustic reed.* <note>original: "lusus ten' calamo agresti" - a reference to the pastoral flute or pipe.</note>

They are in this style and above the pleasant lands. Not with clean horses in <unclear>m.</unclear> lest frequent intrigue should cause happiness to depart out of envy. <note>The commentator appears to be discussing the precarious nature of luck and the envy that followed those who kept their lands.</note> The text says he wonders at the punishment because he had been, or perhaps he is quickly disturbed; they are harshly disturbed without that desert of fault or death. And rightly so, for the times are secretly plucked by narrow circumstances.

Indeed, the true reading is *it is disturbed* <note>original: "turbatur"</note>. This is so it may be an impersonal verb, which pertains to everyone generally. For there had been an expulsion of the Mantuans from their fields <note>Mantua was Virgil's home; its lands were confiscated by Augustus's triumvirate to settle veteran soldiers after the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE.</note>. And if one reads *they are disturbed* <note>original: "turbantur"</note>, the reader seems to refer immediately to the punishments further away, far from the borders. Whence a little later it says: *from here others of us will go to the thirsty Africans* <note>original: "hinc aly sitientes ibim(us) afros" — a quote from Virgil’s Eclogue 1.64, describing the exile of the dispossessed farmers.</note>.

</margin>

For fields are said to bear the hope of the breast, or seeds in the fields. A Region. And excellently in <unclear>beryce</unclear> the steps according to the sons in the naked land; to this pertains those painfully punished. He would look upon it. For they are accustomed to strew grasses for the fearful, as he himself says in the *Georgics*: *And to strew the hard ground with much straw and bundles of fern* <note>original: "Et multa duram stipula filicumq(ue) manuplis sternere humu(m)" — quoting Virgil's Georgics 3.297-298.</note>.

Compare this to that which is a fault released by birth. For by a hiatus they change their mouths <note>A reference to "hiatus," a grammatical term where two vowel sounds meet without a consonant between them.</note>; properly of the earth, it secludes "living things" instead of "excludes" <note>original: "vivas p(ro) excludit" — the commentator is noting a specific word choice where 'living' is used in place of 'hatching' or 'shutting out'.</note>. And the movements were not good, being foolish and varied. And the sense here is: "it ruins us." Note that I argue he was predicting manifest things, but we, with shameless minds, understood how he spoke of the dew of the Tartarean <note>The underworld or hellish regions.</note> depths... <meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Virgil’s first Eclogue, focusing on the symbolic and legal weight of agricultural omens—specifically lightning strikes—and the shepherd Meliboeus’s developing understanding of the power of Rome and Caesar.</meta>

<margin>
The Questioner <note>original: "E Querens."</note>
</margin>

Since Rome is under protection, so that people were once fed by the fruit of this city; just as through the air <note>original: "ayre"</note> and through the lightning bolt, so in Rome, through its own Caesar, damage to a tree signified damage to the fields. Hence, therefore, a tree that is blasted, breathed upon, or lightly struck by lightning <note>In ancient Roman augury, a lightning strike on a tree was a "prodigium" or omen, often signifying divine displeasure regarding the land it stood upon.</note> was a sign; but truly, according to the laws, he who well-founded this city <note>Likely referring to Romulus or Numa Pompilius, the legendary founders of Roman law and religion.</note> sustained the ritual by movement.

<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>

Cicero says that a commander <term>Imperator<explanation>In this context, the commentator refers to the supreme authority or the general's power to oversee the distribution of lands.</explanation></term> is able to cause the fields of those whose trees have been struck by lightning to be lost. In the field, for example, the vines are just as they once were <unclear>four</unclear>. Whether early or late, it shows that such damage will occur as is suffered by trees lightly struck by lightning. And he predicts well, as if speaking and prophesying, so that you may show the augur <note>A religious official who observed and interpreted omens.</note> to be manifest. Why does the listener ask about Caesar? Let him describe Numa. The Latin race belongs to this city, from which it holds everything. Just as the puppies of dogs are similar to the mother, and the kids of goats <note>original: "percussis agnorum hic catulos canis similes sic"</note> are similar to their parents, so he thought Rome differed from other cities not just in size, but in its own standing. He wishes it to be compared to the height of the world, or to the rest of the world, in which one is permitted to see God. When he makes this comparison, comparing the kid to the goats in size, he does not create a dissonance of kind. However, when he says the lion is greater than the dog, he creates a difference in both kind and size, just as he had done regarding the city of Rome.

He says, "I thought that Rome was such a thing to other cities, as a kid is usually compared to goats." For I used to say that it was greater in its own right than the [average] city. But now, truly, I say that it stands apart in every way. For it is the seat of the gods. He proves this by the verse: "As much as the bending viburnums are wont to be among the cypresses." <note>original: "Quantum lenta solent inter viburna cupressi." A famous line from Virgil's first Eclogue where Tityrus compares other cities to small shrubs and Rome to a towering tree.</note> For the viburnum <note>The wayfaring tree, a low-growing shrub.</note> is very short, whereas the cypress is a most lofty tree. 

This way of speaking is found in Varro and in the works of Aristotle; it is also found in Cicero. Why are bodies "bending" or "flexible"? Because they were touched by such great things. To the highest magnitude and excellence of the gods, mortals are compared. From this, as if marveling at the kid, he wishes to have been able to attain liberty <note>original: "libertat"</note> by the grace of justice. Love of liberty—and while others are desirous of liberty in a different way, that free-born man from the <unclear>ravo</unclear> wishes it to be felt here; he wishes to stand by his own will. Just as Virgil...

# Bucolics

Under the persona of the one who says he came to Rome driven by the love of liberty <note>original: "amore libertatis Romā venit impulsus"</note>. And likewise, he subtly criticizes the times in which there was no liberty in the City of Rome; as often as we might correctly and similarly understand in this passage that the shepherd has spoken from the very source of his inspiration. For Virgil wishes to imitate Theocritus; he dresses the character in this way, and to put it briefly, he calls the way of life "to be pastured" <note>original: "via pasci"</note>. Because he looked back upon his own idleness—"Liberty, which though late, looked upon the slothful" <note>quoting Eclogue 1.27: "Libertas, quae sera tamen respexit inertem"</note>—looking back at himself, he wishes to blame his own inactivity for not having come to Rome sooner. And thus, without liberty, the boy <note>likely referring to a slave or servant status</note> is without that which rules this state of advancement.

"Whiter, after..." <note>quoting Eclogue 1.28: "Candidior postquam tondenti barba cadebat" — "Whiter, after the beard fell for me as I was shearing it."</note> <gloss>Or joined</gloss> to the persona, it is as a young man speaking again of bitter things in the Bucolics through allegory. For as we have said, after [so many] years, he wrote the Bucolics. Or should the punctuation <note>original: "distinctio"</note> be correctly changed? So that it is not the beard that is "whiter," but liberty. For after the years... the beard which he had begun to harvest was not grey, and "whiter" fits liberty well. Or we may understand that Virgil was in a state of liberty before, but not of such a kind. 

And after a long time... <note>The text uses abbreviations for the verse: "Et longo post tempore venit" — "And it came after a long time."</note> This whole matter must be investigated, for he mentions a "double time"; he shows when he was moved by liberty, that is, when he began to trim his beard. And having left Galatea, he was held by a most bitter love. Allegorically, however, he says this: "After leaving Mantua <note>Virgil's hometown</note>, I betook myself to Rome." For he wishes Galatea to represent Mantua, and Amaryllis to represent Rome. And he rightly discusses the "times" as if through physical signs <note>original: "quasi instrumentis"</note>, from the beard, in a long discourse after a duration of time.

Either he is most greedy. For the ancients used "after" and "before" <note>original: "post ante"</note> with the ablative case, which today we are least able to do. Or "long after" <note>quoting Eclogue 1.29: "longo post"</note> is one part of the speech, and the sense is: he came here a long time after many [years], and much more after a space of hours than after a long duration. And "long after," as it appears in prospect and purpose, and I will confess, having been driven into it, that this was said through a parenthesis. He hopes for a change... I was not able to preserve my liberty, being oppressed and wavering, but nevertheless, regarding the inheritance of the **Peculium** <term>peculium: the private savings or property that a slave was permitted to accumulate and manage, often used to eventually purchase their freedom</term>. 

Or "peculium" was said in the ancient fashion, because among our ancestors every produce of an estate was named from "cattle" <note>original: "pecudibus"</note>, in which their entire substance and wealth consisted. Whence "money" <note>original: "pecunia"</note> is named after "livestock" <note>original: "pecore"</note>, and this pertains to the customs of those times. For now, we define money as wealth and property, whereas they considered money and wealth to be found in their herds. And it is joined only to this leaf and that which follows, showing the time when liberty at last arrived. Before this, it is as if he records that he had spent his time near Mantua. For "money" <note>original: "pecunia"</note> is used for "savings" <note>original: "peculium"</note> by syncope <term>syncope: a rhetorical or linguistic term for shortening a word by omitting sounds or letters from the middle</term>.

### Regarding the Grove

The service of such a wicked well, or the pomp of the month—or perhaps that which they sacrifice at the end of every month. He gave a response to the first ones who were permitted to live freely forever; before this, none were permitted to graze in such a way, because previously they wandered in meager <note>Latin: *parca*; suggesting a sparse or restricted area</note> pastures; so now let them graze in the meager [pasture].

You perceive a life that is fortunate not merely because of age; it does not matter for the sake of living <note>original: "vivere ly resert"; the writer uses "ly" as a Greek-style definite article</note>, but rather I say it is a fortunate **lineage** <term>propago: a vine-shoot or, metaphorically, a lineage or offspring</term> extending all the way. # The Bucolics

And he praised **Alexis**, whom they say was actually **Alexander**, a slave belonging to **Asinius Pollio** <note>Gaius Asinius Pollio (76 BC – 4 AD): a Roman general, orator, and poet who was one of Virgil's first major patrons</note>. They say Virgil learned to love him to such an extent that in his presence he cherished him as the most beautiful [youth], and eventually received him as a gift. 

He also places the beautiful **Caesar** <note>Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus</note> foremost in wealth and glory. Others think he praises Caesar because of the "true" Caesar <note>original: "verum cesarem"</note> through the persona of Virgil, and that he held a love for boys. Truly, he loved him at that time. 

Others believe the same **Asinius Pollio** was loved by Virgil. For they say that this same person was given as a gift by his master to Virgil, and his name was **Mimpani** <note>original: "mimpani"; likely a scribal corruption of a name from the biographical tradition of Virgil, such as Alexander or perhaps a reference to the youth Cebes</note>. From that kind of love, which is called **ardent** <note>original: "arduales"; likely a transcription error for *ardentis* (burning or passionate)</note>, "sweetly touching Alexis." Truly, they think this was without reason and suspicious; however, this youth was a favorite of Pollio. And Virgil thought he had estimated himself as an equal if he praised the youth's beauty.

<margin>Pollio</margin>

**Pollio** was delighted, as at that time he was pressing upon **Transpadane Italy** <note>The region of Italy north of the Po River</note>, holding power and presiding over the **division of lands** <note>Refers to the confiscation and redistribution of Italian lands to veteran soldiers after the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC</note>. He ought [to say] this because he was indebted to his master—namely, either Caesar or Pollio. 

Lest anyone should hope for the labor [to succeed], nor should hope be placed in it; only in time. **Constantly** <note>original: "Assidue"</note> he brought forth **unrefined** <term>Incondita: unpolished, raw, or rustic verses; literally "not put together"</term>, **uncomposed** things, suddenly spoken: rustic or insane words spoken to the mind, or "soaked" <note>original: "madita"; likely meaning "saturated" with emotion or wine</note> and written down. 

As in **Sallust** <note>The Roman historian Sallust, known for his concise and sometimes archaic style</note>: "Let them approach whom they please." At all this time, he was at the **unrefined gates** <note>original: "portas inconditas"</note>. To the **mountains** and because of the **woods** and his **study** [of poetry], he was boasting; he poured out [his words] in vain, producing nothing for himself, because he was speaking to someone absent. 

In the same way, through an **incongruous allegory** <note>Allegory: a literary device where characters or events represent deeper political or moral meanings</note>, he [describes] **Caesar**, who did not write in the manner of a rhetorician and not...

He gave away the seized lands, and **Alexis** was also moved by contempt. In those cold, marketplace places <note>original: "frigora agora loca"; likely referring to the setting or the cold reception mentioned in the poem</note> is the gem of the serpent. **Thestylis** is the name of a rustic woman who prepares a pottage for the reapers when they are exhausted by the heat, by crushing various types of herbs. This is either a type of food, a seasoning, or something "tessellated" <note>original: "tessalit"; likely a corruption of the text referring to the mixing or pounding of ingredients</note>. 

This is a common name among country folk. Because of this, she was in those rustic parts for those who were weary and burning, exhausted by the vehement heat. She uses **wild thyme** <note>original: "serpillum"</note> and other pungent herbs like **squill** <note>original: "scilla"; a flowering plant in the asparagus family used medicinally</note>—strong herbs that repel the heat. For etc.

<margin>Pliny: Book 20</margin>

As **Pliny** says in his *Natural History* <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of a massive encyclopedia of the ancient world</note>: Medicine [works] either by opposites or by what can be taken in, whereby heat is driven out either by cold or by another heat. Regarding this, in his final Eclogue, the lover seeks a remedy for his passion for a long time. We use these [remedies] either for cold or for the heat of **Ethiopia**, as the intensity of the Ethiopians is felt under the **constellation of Cancer** <note>The zodiac sign associated with the summer solstice and peak heat</note>.

Certainly, **wild thyme** is the herb which they also call *herpillon* in **Greek**. For in many noted cases, where there is an aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note> in Greek, we [Latin speakers] use the letter **S** in place of that aspiration. Hence, *herpillon* becomes **serpyllum** <note>wild thyme</note>, *hex* becomes **six** <note>original: "sex"</note>, and *hepta* becomes **seven** <note>original: "septem"</note>. 

"Rapid" is used here to mean vehement or burning. They are said to be "weary" from either the heat or the labor of preparation. 

<note>The following section discusses "hyperbaton," a rhetorical device where the normal word order is disrupted for emphasis.</note>

If it were *adiperid* <note>likely a scribal error for a Greek grammatical term</note>, it would be a **hyperbaton** <term>hyperbaton: a figure of speech where words that naturally belong together are separated</term>, as in: "while I track your footsteps." 

"The orchards ring for me" <note>a quote from Eclogue 2, line 12</note>; for so much comes out of it, but it is better to ask: "but what is it?" and so let us understand it this way: **Thestylis** carries the crushed herbs for the reapers, and meanwhile, the orchards ring out with the sound of the cicadas <note>the text mentions "farris," likely a corruption referring to the grain or the buzzing of insects in the fields</note>. Regarding the word **Thestylis**, the author added the "t" sound to it, as is often done, just as in the words *terennum* or *amarium*.

### Pastoral Commentary: Eclogue II

This is a question of love, as he well knows; it shows not only the one who has become accustomed to something in this place, whence **Horace** <note>The Roman lyric poet (65–8 BC)</note> speaks of the "pleasing boldness of the good" <note>original: "boni grata protervitas"</note>, rising above distains. And from disdain comes all pride. "Was it not Menalcas...?" <note>Virgil, Eclogue 2.15</note>.

<margin>Alexander</margin>
It is said that **Corydon** loved **Alexander**, whom **Iollas** gave to him—the same boy whom those "born for love" <note>original: "amorenatos"; likely referring to poets or lovers</note> say preferred the boy **Cebetes**.

<margin>Cebetes</margin>
<margin>Lera</margin>
Whose girl was **Lera**. Because of this, some wish to understand the name **Amaryllis** as representing **Lesbia**, and **Menalcas** as representing **Cebetes**.

<margin>Donatus</margin>
"O handsome boy" <note>original: "O formose puer"; Eclogue 2.17</note>. **Donatus** <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian and Virgil commentator</note> rightly says that he speaks by suspending and then persuading the boy of his beauty, so that you may understand he desired something else for such a one; but he speaks "in the grass" <note>in the rustic setting</note> lest he should offend the discourse and the judgment of love.

<margin>Sallust</margin>
...Scarcely return, do not trust. In **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian</note> they saw the health of youth... "The white privets fall" <note>original: "Alba ligustra cadunt"; Eclogue 2.18. Virgil uses this to show that even beautiful white flowers are discarded while dark hyacinths are gathered</note>. Both rustic and amorous people make comparisons from flowers. The **privet** <note>term: ligustrum; a shrub with white flowers</note> is a white flower of very little value; but "**vaccinia**" <note>term: vaccinia; often translated as hyacinths or blueberries</note> are indeed violets which are of a purple color.

<margin>}<image-desc>A large curly bracket on the right margin groups the following four lines of text.</image-desc></margin>
It is manifest that he says there are things in which lovers can boast, both for beauty and for song, which he seems to recount in order. And much with the "honor of the seat" <note>likely referring to the status or location of the lover</note>... but it is better that he finds "two of the flock." Nor do the sheep fall, being in great number; whence we read in the ***Georgics*** <note>Virgil's later poem on agriculture</note>: "Immediately choose for them flocks with white soft wool" <note>original: "Continuo greges illis lege mollibus albos"</note>. 

Also elsewhere: "Now thus on the bare [ground]... to believe oneself worthy." "A thousand of my sheep [wander in the Sicilian mountains]" <note>original: "Mille meae Siculis errant in montibus agnae"; Eclogue 2.21</note>. They were either grazing in the wild, or are praised for the waters and the hedges, just as they are praised for their age.

For as he might speak with you among the flocks, a more abundant supply comes forth than you might be harmed by, not only in summer but even in the snow <note>Referring to Virgil, Eclogue 2.22: "My fresh milk fails not in summer nor in winter."</note>. **Amphion** of Dirce on **Actaea** <note>Referring to Eclogue 2.24: "Amphion Dircaeus in Actaeo Aracyntho"</note>. This is understood because **Amphion** and **Zethus** were the sons of **Jupiter** and **Antiope**. But **Zethus** was a man of the countryside, whereas **Amphion** was so skilled in the musical arts that he <unclear>moved</unclear> the walls and the people of **Thebes** with his song. The term **Dircean** is said to come from the Greek for the moon <note>The commentator is likely confused here; Dirce was a famous fountain in Thebes</note>, from which we ought to understand the "coastal arts," as they say that in the solitary land of **Evander** <note>The hero who founded the city on the site of future Rome</note> there was a shore, though not specifically at **Athens**. Although the arts were first brought to Athens, the arts are often said to be received at **Aracynthus** <note>A mountain on the border of Boeotia and Attica</note> near Athens. This is not because they were discovered at Athens, but to show the lack of skill of the country folk. Where **Theocritus** speaks to express an infinite simplicity, he says many things differently than a voice normally would, using this name for the place.

**Oaxis** must certainly be understood as a river <note>Eclogue 2.66 refers to the "rapid Oaxis"</note>, although it is also a mountain, as we said above. "Nor am I so ugly..." <note>original: "Nec sum adeo informis"; Eclogue 2.25</note>. In truth, while the sea was calm, he looked at himself in the ocean. For a person to see that they are not deformed by nature, he did not want to call himself "most beautiful," but rather used the modest phrase "not ugly" while standing on the shore.

That is, concerning him who is <unclear>shaggy</unclear> or who has a giant eye—the **Cyclops**—or perhaps because it is a river in the first place.

# Bucolics

...from which [it follows] that some play on the shore in water left behind by rivers in a pool. From this, a person could have seen [themselves], because that [circumstance] rules out [distortion] **when the sea stood calm, untroubled by winds** <note>Referring to Virgil, Eclogue 2.26: "cum placidum ventis staret mare"</note>. But in the sea, an image is not usually retained because the wind blows; for if it stood still, it would not fail to return an image to us in all respects.

<margin>Daphnis</margin>
**I am not Daphnis** <note>Eclogue 2.26: "nec cum Daphnide ego". Corydon compares himself to the legendary shepherd Daphnis</note>. Daphnis was the son [of Mercury], the most beautiful of youths, I believe, who was the first to be a shepherd in **Sicily** <note>original: "Inctiuo", likely a corruption of "Siculo"</note>. **If the image does not deceive me.** Nothing of a god's creation <note>or "no thing"</note> deceives in such a way as an image; for even in a mirror it shows everything distorted, and in water a whole thing is seen as if it were **broken** <note>original: "fractum"</note>, which **Cicero** also teaches more fully in his *Academics* <note>original: "in insulanis"; referring to Cicero's discussion of optical illusions, such as a straight oar appearing broken in water</note>. "With you as judge," he would say of himself, "you who would despise my beauty." **That the foul countryside might please you** <note>Eclogue 2.28: "O tantum libeat mecum tibi sordida rura"</note>. That you might be pleased to dwell for a time in the countryside which is "foul" to you; that is, which you *think* is foul. For where is the artisan here? I dwell much better; that [feeling of belonging] comes when I dwell in that thing of which we speak. For he also pronounced the word for this incorrectly... <note>The commentator here begins a technical grammatical digression on the verb "to dwell"</note>

<margin>In habit/dwelling</margin>
...from that matter of **habititude** <note>original: "habititudine"; referring to one's condition or way of living</note>, they fix their [possessions], or it had been what they fix for the support of the cottage, which he says through the likeness of them... <unclear>reommo[n]d</unclear> of stags. Or, what is better, to flee hunting crows. To **throw the javelin** <note>original: "Iaculari"</note> more for pleasure, that is, what is seen to change for his own labor.

<margin>Hibiscus</margin>
Charmingly, **with the hibiscus** <note>Eclogue 2.30: "haedorumque gregem viridi compellere hibisco"</note>. Pertaining to the hibiscus, "having driven [the kids] with the hibiscus." It is a type of herb. And thus he says **with the hibiscus**, referring to the hibiscus plant. As also the shout of the farmer... by the example found too much in the rough places...

His horns are in imitation of the **rays of the sun**, and the horn from this...

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of Virgil’s Second Eclogue. The commentator is now interpreting the figure of Pan, moving from the visual allegory of his body to the mythological origins of his pipe, and finally to the grammatical properties of his name in Latin.</meta>

For he sees a likeness, as his face is made in imitation of the **ether** <note>The upper atmosphere or heavens</note>; on his breast he likewise has a starry dappling <note>original: "stellatũ"; likely referring to the *nebris* or fawn-skin often worn by Pan, symbolizing the stars</note>. Because the upper part is most like the stars, the entire lower part is shaggy because of the trees, brushwood, and wild beasts. He has **goat's feet** to show the solidity of the earth. He holds a **pipe of seven reeds** <note>The *fistula* or pan-pipe</note> because of the **harmony of the heavens** <note>original: "armonia celi"</note>, in which there are seven sounds. In this same [instrument], through seven distinct pipes, he is musical; through this, it is described how the cycle of the year <note>original: "p annũ"</note> returns into itself through all of nature. He is said to have played for a singular love, through which we read: **Love conquers all** <note>Virgil, Eclogue 10.69: "Omnia vincit amor"</note>. Therefore, Pan, according to the myths,

<margin>Syrinx</margin>
is said to have loved the nymph **Syrinx**. When he pursued her, she implored the help of the earth and was turned into reeds. From these, Pan, as a solace for his love, cut [them] and made a pipe for himself. It should be known that the name **Pan** <note>original: "pana"</note> is an authentic Greek monosyllable which, having passed into our language, is declined in various cases. In the ablative and dative plurals, both syllables are used, such as *panos* and *pani* <note>The commentator is discussing how to adapt the Greek name *Pan* into Latin grammar</note>. These two have an accent, even if they cannot fully pass into our usage. **Do not let it permit** <note>A commentary on Eclogue 2.34: "nec te paeniteat calamo trivisse labellum" (nor let it shame you to have worn your lip on the reed)</note>. Let it not seem too little to you. **Gluttonous** <note>original: "Edax"</note>. But if anything is done here in this work, it seems to be permitted through Pan. And it should be noted that "permit" was used in place of the present tense... as much as is allowed in defective verbs... as the mind itself dreads to remember. For in this little story of labor, what does the **ape** <note>original: "simia"; perhaps a metaphor for imitation or a commentary on the physical movement of the lips</note> attempt to do in its dissection, so that the two lips might be called "waves of lips"? What makes us so very many who do not comply and are forced by this affect of the high-maned one? Arrange the seven...

# . The Bucolics <note>original: "Buc." for *Bucolica*</note>

Grace takes hold when nature follows. For since indignation is the freedom to then be what exists among all newly discovered and revealed things, and especially when things are joined together. And he speaks rightly, for concerning these things, the world consumes <note>original: "Comedat mundu’"; likely a reference to how the passage of time or the world wears things away</note> what is given through inheritance. And because constant industry obtains a thing, gifts are given with difficulty by the givers, yet once received, they are easily found [precious] by the world. Nor does "found in a dangerous valley" <note>Referring to Eclogue 2.40: *tuta mihi valle reperti*</note> merely commend them; it highlights the difficulty of the task here in the first part. Nor are they received as any longer whole from the burning sun. For the dappling on their white skins, while there are still spots worthy of their age, vigorously suits them; then they imitate the color, and the spots show that they have earned their stay. "Body," he says here. And then for you: **young goats** <note>original: "capreolos"</note> who still have white dappled skins, whom I am even now keeping for you; whom I keep for you even though **Thestylis** <note>A female servant or fellow rustic in the Eclogues</note>, my friend, asks for them and desires to lead them away from me. "She shall lead them away," he says, or "let her lead them away." This is a figure of speech regarding gifts: one gives so that he may have [favor]. And he does this because he did not want to say "And let her do it," lest he should offend the one he loved if he had said he wished to give the value to another; but he had prepared this for him: **Come here, O beautiful boy; for you the nymphs bring lilies in full baskets.** <note>Virgil, Eclogue 2.45-46: "huc ades, o formose puer: tibi lilia plenis / ecce ferunt Nymphae calathis"</note> Honor yourself for the boy with song, and he speaks of the things to be presented. Certainly, **baskets** <note>original: "calathis"</note> is a Greek word.

<margin>£ Basket <note>original: "Calathus"</note></margin>
<margin>£ Wool-basket <note>original: "Quasill’"</note></margin>
For in Latin it is called a **wool-basket** <note>original: "quasillum"</note>. As Curio says in the *Philippics* <note>A reference to Cicero’s *Philippic* orations, which often satirized the effeminacy or domestic scandals of his rivals</note>, "among the golden wool-baskets of cloth."

<margin>Nais</margin>
**White Nais** <note>A water nymph mentioned in Eclogue 2.46</note>, either beautiful or a goddess-nymph. She will enter to be celebrated, for they are seen to be ungrateful; hence she is changed into a "white stitching." Whence also he speaks of **pale violets** <note>original: "Pallentis violae"; Eclogue 2.47</note>. He says this because lovers are accustomed to grow pale. The color of the lover changes.

<margin>Oratory <note>original: "Orat’"</note></margin>
Horace: "And then that paleness of lovers, like the wood-violet." <note>original: "viola pallor amantium"; referencing Horace, Odes 3.10.14. The "pale" violet (viola pallida) was actually a yellowish-white flower, matching the sallow complexion thought to affect those in love.</note> Whence it is not without affection.

Anethum <note>original: "Anethu"; dill or anise</note>.

The nymphs offer these flowers to the gods of lovers, flowers which are themselves similar to lovers. Truly, the poppy and the **Narcissus**; for Narcissus had been a most beautiful boy who was transformed into the flower of his own name. By offering this, he [Corydon] gives a reminder, as if to say that something of this nature should be given to this one [Alexis] for the sake of a single love. Then there is **cassia**, a herb of the sweetest scent, and the things that follow which indicate what some call cassia. And as it is said, "then cassia and other sweet herbs are intermingled," just as one reads in Sallust <note>The commentator is comparing Virgil's use of "cassia" with other Roman authors like Sallust to establish botanical or poetic consistency</note> that it brings other things.

**He paints the soft hyacinths with yellow marigold** <note>original: "Mollia luteola pingit vaccinia caltha"; Virgil, Eclogue 2.50</note>

They compose the "painting" of soft hyacinths <note>original: "vaccinia"; often interpreted as blueberries or dark hyacinths</note> from the yellow marigold. For if "yellow" <note>original: "luteola"</note> were in a different grammatical case to the observer, they might not understand the verse. He says "soft" or "yellow" for many reasons, of course. And he says this: he seeks adornment from the diversity of colors.

**Hoary... with downy... fruit** <note>original: "Cana .l. lani. mala"; referring to Virgil's "cana legam tenera lanugine mala," meaning quinces</note> he says, that is, **quinces** <note>original: "cydonia"</note> which are full of downy fuzz; but this is not because of their length. For even in a corrected version, it is more worthy among those residing [in the text]. In the past, it was rumored that those who were lovers were not loved in return. And regarding the shameful thing, which the Rhetorician mentions as an apothegm <note>original: "apote"; likely "apophthegma," a concise saying or maxim</note>.

**And chestnuts** <note>original: "Castaneas q; nuces"</note> I hope for well. He added "two chestnuts." For "nuts" includes all kinds of fruit enclosed in a harder shell, such as hazelnuts, almonds, and acorns. Chestnuts, like all of these, are the softest among them.

**Which my Amaryllis used to love** <note>original: "Mea quā Amaryllis amabat"</note>. He would not want it to seem he only chose chestnuts because he loved them himself, but because they were favored by her [Amaryllis]. He deemed that they should flourish in her honor. And from the plum or toward the scent of these two soft things; you, the laurel, praise the branches, and it shall be an honor.

<meta>This page continues the technical and allegorical analysis of Virgil’s works, moving from the general classification of poetic styles into specific commentary on the Third and Tenth Eclogues. It focuses on the distinction between the voice of the poet and the voices of his characters.</meta>

The poet speaks in the **mixed** style <note>Latin: *mixtum*; a style where both the author and characters speak</note>, which is to say, a mixture as found in comedies and tragedies, and as it is in the *Aeneid*. For there, both the poet speaks and characters are introduced who speak. All these various styles are contained within the *Bucolics*, and the poems are demonstrated as such in their books.

For this work is **exegematic** <note>narrative or descriptive style where the poet speaks in his own voice</note>, where the poet speaks according to the prayers of the Muse. From here comes the impulse and the beginning: *“Grant me this last labor, Arethusa”* <note>original: "hunc arethusa mihi"; a reference to the opening of Eclogue X</note>.

It also possesses the **dramatic** style <note>Latin: *dragmaticum*; where characters speak directly to one another</note>, as seen in the first Eclogue. In this style, the poet intensely explains the affairs of lovers in their proper order. Here, in this very place—as if in the first of all the sacred books—he treats the injury of deeds, and from that, how the possessors might maintain their constancy; the scorn that follows is where the sentiment originates regarding what he says is loved by Gallus.

<margin>Whose?</margin> **“Whose flock?”** <note>original: "Cuius pecus"; the opening of Eclogue III</note> is said out of bitterness. For by calling it a "flock," he shows him to be a man of miseries. Regarding the word *cuium* <note>an archaic form of "whose"</note>, the ancients declined it in all forms, just as "discolored" is used for the person of a friend, which is now a common usage. The ancients used to say *megnia* for "mine," and *memus*, just as they used *tui* and *tua* for "yours." 

It is not only **Arethusa** whom he speaks of loving; here the flock is vital to him. And he spoke to him of bitter things and showed him in two parts. There are two parts to this, if anyone knows how to distinguish them: among all the things handed down, only love holds a common bond for lovers, as the Muse has handed down.

The order is "unhappy": **“O always unhappy flock!”** 

<margin>Neaera.</margin> The sheep are always the flock, while he himself cherishes **Neaera**, his girlfriend. He becomes a stranger to his own sheep while he fondles her; while he prefers her embrace, the flock is neglected. It is as if he were saying that from the moment she departs, he takes up the task, especially if the master himself is absent. 

**“He milks them twice in an hour”** <note>A reference to Eclogue III, line 5, where a rival shepherd is accused of stealing milk</note>, because the light remains throughout the whole day for all these fears to occur. For as a matter of praise in the *Georgics*, it is possible **“to milk the sheep twice a day.”** Truly, as the day rises, he milks the hours.

And in the feminine gender we say "this milking-pail" <note>original: "hec mulctra"</note> and in the neuter gender "these milking-pails" <note>original: "horum mulctra"</note>, which is why it is said in the *Georgics*: **"The cows will fill the milking-pails."** <note>A reference to Virgil's *Georgics* 3.177, discussing the productivity of the herd.</note> Others make a distinction so that "to milk" <note>original: "mulctare"</note> refers to the time when animals are milked, while the "milking-pail" is that in which they are milked. **I stake** <note>original: "depono"</note>: I place as a wager, I signify; and it is seen in <unclear>Ausonius</unclear> <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a 4th-century Roman poet and teacher</note> that which was mentioned above, regarding when someone gives birth. He says "milking-pail" so that for a long time much is given through joined names. This is a general epithet <note>original: "epiteton"</note>, a naming here which is called "one head of livestock" <note>original: "vna pecus"</note> and it draws toward the person and everything from which they come. Otherwise, even today, some incorrectly do not accept it. We say "the other" <note>original: "alter"</note> regarding two things, not regarding three; from which "the other" is understood concerning the neutral one. Nor should it move us that he spoke otherwise of the woman; for in implying names that we cannot say, "the woman" is also spoken of regarding two.

### The Eclogues

Among the ancestors, the birthday <note>original: "natalis"</note> was fully observed on the appointed days. Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a Roman poet</note> spoke of this honor. Juvenal says the "Birthday is a grateful gift." On a day neighboring my birthday, sweet to me... <note>original: "Natali vicinus die mihi dulcis"; referencing the timing of the celebration.</note> When you sacrifice... <note>original: "cum sacrificaveris"</note> And marking the festival with a heifer <note>original: "vitulam"; the female calf intended for sacrifice</note>, he says, "so that I may perform your rites." <note>A reference to line 77: "cum faciam vitula pro frugibus, ipse venito" (when I sacrifice a heifer for the crops, come yourself).</note>
At that hour, water cannot [be used?]. Regarding this evil <note>original: "mali"; possibly referring to a ritual prohibition</note>, it is said that before this sacrifice one walks around
<margin>Ambarvalia <note>original: "Carnabale"; clearly a corruption of "Ambarvale," the festival for purifying the fields.</note></margin>
and the victim goes around with water. As he himself <note>Virgil</note> says in the *Georgics*: "Thrice let the lucky victim go around the new crops." This is just like the *Amburbale* or *Amburbium* <term>Amburbium: A Roman ritual of purification where the sacrificial victims were led in a procession around the boundaries of the city (urbs).</term>. It is called a sacrifice because the victim circles and encompasses the city.
Damoetas says... here the shepherd either has two names, just as
<margin>Palaemon <note>original: "pola."</note></margin>
he said above regarding the same Menalcas; or certainly he refers to Palaemon, whom they call, as it were, the best shepherd. This is from a most noble shepherd, just as we call an anonymous or plebeian lot a servant or an adult <note>The OCR "adultorium" is likely "adjutorem" (helper) or "adulterium".</note> but little.
For at length the "balista" <note>likely a corruption of the line "longum 'formose, vale, vale'"</note> or from the horn he shouts; he used the word as an adverb. "Farewell, farewell" <note>original: "balé balé"; phonetic transcription of the Latin "vale, vale" from line 79.</note> he said, he began, if indeed it is a vowel, as in "I laugh at you, O Alope." He testifies to a sad thing: "sweet, sweet enough." <note>Refers to line 80: "triste lupus stabulis... dulce satis umor" (The wolf is a sad thing for the stalls... moisture is sweet for the crops).</note> The crops are for those weaned from milk <note>original: "depulsis a lacte"</note>, forbidden from milk, as those "driven from milk."
<margin>Pollio</margin>
...the gift [for] which he would shut up the lambs. "Pollio loves [our Muse, though she is rustic]" <note>Eclogue 3, line 84: "Pollio amat nostram, quamvis est rustica, Musam."</note>. He flatters. Now he mentions Pollio <note>Gaius Asinius Pollio, a Roman statesman, orator, and poet</note> as a writer of tragedies and histories, which Horace also testifies to.

...as if through certain mounds. <margin>.Suetonius.</margin> Indeed, this question is varied. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Virgil's *Bucolics*, specifically moving into the "Fourth Eclogue," often called the Messianic Eclogue. The previous page concluded the third Eclogue and began the introduction to this new, more elevated poem dedicated to Asinius Pollio.</meta>

With the help of **Virgil** <note>The commentator refers to the author in the third person here, discussing his stylistic choices</note> he imitates, as we said above:

->**Let us sing of somewhat greater things**<-
<note>original: "Paulo maiora canamus"; the famous opening of Eclogue 4, signaling a shift from lowly pastoral themes to a more "epic" style</note>

It is well said, "let us sing of somewhat greater things," for although this eclogue departs from the usual [pastoral] tone—being of a rarer sort—he nevertheless inserts into it certain things appropriate to the work. These Virgilian mixtures are very humble at the end, and beyond...

<margin>The Cumaean Sibyl</margin>
**The [last] age of the song comes** <note>original: "Ultima Cumaei venit iam carminis aetas"; referring to the prophecy of the Sibyl regarding the cycle of history</note>. The **Sibyl** was from **Cumae** <note>A priestess of Apollo at the Greek colony of Cumae in Italy, famous for her prophecies</note>, and she divided the ages of the world according to metals <note>The "Ages of Man" concept: Gold, Silver, Bronze, and Iron</note>. He says, therefore, who rules in which age, and declares that there is only one king or god. He names him from **Apollo**, whence he says: **now your Apollo reigns** <note>original: "tuus iam regnat Apollo"</note>. There are, therefore, certain fixed ages. Regarding how these are renewed, the authorities here disagree; they conclude by saying that when the **Great Year** <term>Magnus Annus: an astronomical cycle where the sun, moon, and planets all return to the same relative positions, believed by ancients to trigger a total reset of human history</term> is completed, all the stars return to their original starting point and bring back their same motions. This is the "maturity of the stars," so that all things which have been shall have a universal repetition; this is known from the manifest movement of the stars. Following this, **Virgil** says a new age has come: all things that were are repeated, and once again there shall be a measure of the ages through the ages.

<margin>Erigone</margin>
**And the Virgin comes** <note>original: "iam redit et Virgo"; referring to Astraea or Justice</note>, namely **Justice**, who was **Erigone** <note>In Greek myth, Erigone was transformed into the constellation Virgo; her return signifies the return of the Golden Age</note>. And he promised the praise of both the boy and of the consulship—that is, of **Augustus** <note>The commentator here interprets the "prophesied child" of the poem as the future Emperor Augustus, though the poem is dedicated to Pollio</note>. For the happiness of the times pertains to the praise of the Emperor. **Now a new progeny is sent down from high heaven** <note>original: "Iam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto"</note>, so that these men might seem not born of mortals but of divinities, and as if fallen from heaven. And from this, it sounds as if there will be a **Golden Age**, because **Augustus** the Emperor is the one for whom such a boy is born; he favors the one being born for the sake of **Pollio**.

<margin>
Lucina
Diana
Juno
</margin>
**Lucina** <note>The goddess of childbirth</note>. For he says that **Lucina** favors him, she who will change the ages from iron to gold. **Smile then, chaste Lucina; now your Apollo reigns** <note>original: "Casta fave Lucina tuus iam regnat Apollo"</note>. Thus **Horace** <note>A contemporary poet and friend of Virgil</note> <unclear>then</unclear> proves that you are called **Lucina**. He said that **Juno** was **Lucina**, just as **Juno**...

<margin>The Sibyl</margin>
[The poet mentions Lucina] either as the **Moon** or as **Ops** <note>original: "lunna seu opem"; the commentator is debating the identity of Lucina, the goddess of childbirth mentioned in the poem. She is often identified with Diana (the Moon) or Ops (an earth goddess of plenty)</note>. Since both are deities... then **now Apollo reigns** <note>original: "iam regit apollo"; Eclogue 4.10. The sun god Apollo was the patron of Augustus</note>. And regarding the "Foster Child" <note>original: "Alumnu"; likely referring to the child whose birth is predicted in the poem</note>, according to **Servius** <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century commentator whose notes were essential for medieval readers of Virgil</note>, he shows that the **Sibyl** is usually remembered [in this context] and he touches upon **Augustus**, whose statues were ordered to be made with the insignia of **Apollo**. He introduces the beginning; he dares, that is, he begins to know and foresee that the **great [months]** <note>original: "magnū... mtessē" / "magnum procedere menses"</note> are to begin.

That [passage] touches upon the fact that the months of **July** and **August** received their names in honor of Augustus [and Julius Caesar]. For previously they were called **Quintilis** and **Sextilis** <note>The fifth and sixth months of the old Roman calendar</note>. And this also serves as an argument: **with you as leader** <note>original: "te duce"; Eclogue 4.13</note>, whether referring to Augustus or **Pollio** <note>Asinius Pollio, the Roman consul to whom Virgil dedicated this poem</note>, or the **traces of our crime** <note>original: "sceleris vestigia"; Virgil refers to the "remnants of our guilt," meaning the civil wars</note>. It is well said: does no one want to be the prince... on the earth? That is, he speaks of the remaining things and the power he holds over his superiors.

When he was praising Augustus and had set forth the transition to Augustus... through a winding order... they bear arms against the cities. They rage with the full force of war through the whole world. He describes bold things... and does not hear... in order to show that the remaining evils of the past were so great that they might not even seem able to be calmed by the best of winds.

# Bucolics

He will **receive the life of the gods** <note>original: "deum vita accipiet"; Eclogue 4.15</note>. Above, he skillfully displays praise and considers to whom he should refer this: either to **Augustus** or to **Saloninus** <note>Saloninus was the son of Asinius Pollio; many early commentators debated whether Virgil meant a son of the Roman elite or a divine figure like Augustus</note> who was prepared as a patron of both worlds. Or he refers it to Augustus; or Saloninus, through the virtue of Pollio, held the world. These are the lines. It is praise for both the one who swore the oath and the one who prepared for it.

Then: **But for you, boy, the earth will pour out its first little gifts without cultivation** <note>original: "At tibi prima puer nullo munuscula cultu telluris"; Eclogue 4.18. Virgil describes nature providing for the child automatically, without the need for farming, signaling a return to the Golden Age</note>. He does not foresightedly assume these [gifts] at the very beginning of the boy's virtue, but they come gradually, almost at last, with age. These **little gifts** rightly shine for the well-deserving.

<margin>
Ivy
Baccaris
</margin>
This occurs while the earth was present everywhere. He gathers **ivy** wandering here and there along with **baccaris** <note>original: "baccare"; an aromatic plant, possibly foxglove or sowbread, believed to protect against the evil eye</note>. From this, the men of old called ivies "flowing feet" <note>original: "fluia pedes"</note> because they wander this way and that. He praises the boy through these very gifts. For **ivy** should clothe the greatest poet, so that they may adorn the poet with the budding ivy. **Baccaris**, however, is a herb that wards off **enchantment** <note>original: "fascinum"; the evil eye or a malevolent spell</note>; you should adorn your forehead with baccaris so that it does not harm the seer <note>original: "vati"; referring to the poet as a prophetic "vates"</note>.

The praise in this lies in the fact that they [the plants] do not return [to their wild state] themselves. Nor is it more in another. Goodness persists in moderation. **What great lions will there be** <note>original: "magnī leones"; Eclogue 4.22. In the Golden Age, predators will not be a threat</note>.

# Bucolics 4

<margin>
Amomum
Assyria
</margin>

**Assyrian [balsam]** <note>original: "Assyrium... amomum"; Virgil, Eclogue 4.25</note> is commonly called **amomum**; it is an herb of the sweetest scent which grows only in Assyria. Everywhere and commonly, he "now reads the praises of herbs and the deeds of his parents" <note>original: "herbarum laudes et facta parentum iam legit"; referencing line 26</note>. The better sense is that along with the virtues of all the herbs, he also learns the virtues of his parents. Thus he will be able to recognize virtue as it approaches, and he will acknowledge the glory of all things. He added the word **wandering** <note>original: "errante"</note>, but hiddenly; and by a deceptive pact they correspond to their own times, as he explains.

<margin>Tethys</margin>
**A few things** <note>original: "pauca"</note>. **Which prompted men to tempt Tethys** <note>original: "quae temptare Thetym"; line 31. Tethys was a sea goddess, here used as a poetic term for the sea</note>, that is, the sea. He shows that navigation is a product of foresight, though they forbid it as if it were a great boast. For through navigation, he shows that there will be greed, which compels men to sail through the waves.

<margin>(by its own)</margin>
It signifies by its own <note>original: "suis"</note> star. Through the **North Wind** <note>original: "aquilone"</note> he thus shows fear.

<margin>
Tiphys
Argo
Achilles
</margin>
**There will then be another Tiphys** <note>original: "alter erit tum Tiphys"; line 34. Tiphys was the pilot of the Argo, the first ship in Greek myth</note>. These specifically refer to the ancestors. For by **Tiphys**, we understand any pilot; by the **Argo**, we understand any ship; by **Troy**, any city; and by **Achilles**, any man who is good and brave. 

This seems to be spoken here broadly through **apocatastasis** <term>apocatastasis: a Greek philosophical concept of "restoration" where the universe returns to its original state</term>, that is, through the revolution of all things and the return of the stars to their starting point. Or we say as above: **The traveler himself shall give up the sea** <note>original: "cedet mari vector"; line 38</note>, and if ever trade is omitted, **the whole earth shall produce all things** <note>original: "omnis feret omnia tellus"; line 39</note>. We judge that navigation will become rare. 

**The wool shall lose its deceptive color** <note>original: "desinet mentiri lana colores"; line 42</note> when the sheep are dyed with variety. From what heavenly juice are they dyed? **The purple changes** <note>original: "purpura mutat"</note>; they are dyed instead of the natural **mud-yellow** color <note>original: "luteo colore"</note> we have seen. And there is an **hypallage** <term>hypallage: a rhetorical device where a modifier is shifted from the noun it logically describes to another</term> for "new mud-yellow." For saffron is a mud-yellow color, from which also "aluta" <note>a type of soft leather dyed with madder or saffron</note> is named. **Sandyx** <note>original: "sandix"; line 45</note> is the herb from which we say the color is dyed. 

**"Run, such ages," the Fates said to their spindles** <note>original: "talia saecla suis dixerunt currite fusis... Parcae"; line 46-47</note>. Let the Fates agree with a unified preparation. Now the goddesses have spoken; the stars are the established decrees of the fates of men. What has once been spoken remains stable, for the boundaries are shared and unchanging.

He, however, promised that he would first go to arrange his affairs and would then return for the wedding. Thus, when Demophon delayed his return, Phyllis—driven by the impatience of love and the grief of believing herself rejected—ended her life with a noose. She was then transformed into an **almond tree** <term>amygdalum</term> without leaves. Later, when Demophon returned and learned what had happened, he embraced the tree; it is said that the tree, as if sensing the arrival of its bridegroom, burst forth with leaves. From this, those leaves were named "phylla" after Phyllis, whereas they were previously called "petala" <note>This is a classic folk etymology: the Greek word for leaf, *phyllon*, is linked here to the name Phyllis.</note>. Regarding this man [Daphnis], known from here even to the stars: namely, at least as far as he seems to be seen in the estimation of the expert. To this man the pain of death has arrived. He foresees those who, although they wander, take care lest they then lack fruit; he joyfully approves with cruelty through <unclear>a man</unclear>, for which reason I know not, because it is incredible; he proves it by testimony, said this, and moves to where they speak of the river. 

But what does it mean when he says "no witnesses" and the "rivers"? It is interpreted as: "The Road" witnesses, but the "rivers" do not speak. For when these send the best mentor into themselves and are seen to act. But as for the witnesses of <margin>men.</margin> new men, neither can these witnesses say from where, by definition, we can say that witnesses of death are those who see. The hazels and the rivers. <margin>livestock.</margin> It is of the hours. A witness on the journey by the river; properly, the stars are witnesses for us. These things, however, which were about to be lifted up, cease with death, having embraced his miserable body; it is the lament of the son, and from the body here there is nothing.

# The Bucolics:

A poem of two verses is called an **interlude** <term>intermedium</term> <note>original: "intermium"; referring to the alternating structure of the song between the two shepherds, Mopsus and Menalcas.</note> because a single tone is spoken from one poem, as if the poem might conquer by a sign. <margin><unclear>intercl.</unclear></margin>

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on Virgil’s works, specifically transitioning into the Sixth Eclogue of the Bucolics. It discusses the poet’s shift from ambitious epic themes to the refined "Syracusan" style of pastoral poetry, guided by the god Apollo.</meta>

# The Bucolics

**"My Muse first deigned to play in Syracusan verse,"** <note>original: "Prima syracuso dignata est ludere versu"; this is the opening line of Virgil's Sixth Eclogue, where he establishes his debt to the Greek poet Theocritus.</note> and our Roman Muse did not blush to inhabit the woods. Just as he was an imitator of **Theocritus of Syracuse** <note>Theocritus was the 3rd-century BC Greek creator of pastoral poetry; "Syracosio" refers to his home in Sicily.</note>, he had destined himself to write bucolic poetry. Previously, among the learned, it was called Syracusan in Latin—where the "y" is Roman. You too are a Muse of fate. She "deigned," which is to say she was, as if from a higher place, willing to dwell in the woods, just as some are willing to live in humble cottages. **Thalia** <note>The Muse of comedy and pastoral poetry.</note> was the Muse in Greek, or Thalea in Latin; she ought to have led the song like a dance <note>original: "orcheria," likely referring to *orchesis* or choral dance.</note>, but for the sake of euphony, she was constrained by her own rules and so remained in a state of balance.

**"When I was singing of kings and battles,"** <note>original: "Cum canerent reges et prelia"; Eclogue 6.3. Virgil suggests he initially tried to write epic poetry about historical wars.</note> **Cynthius** <note>An epithet for Apollo, derived from Mount Cynthus on the island of Delos where he was born.</note> <unclear>plucked my ear</unclear>. This signifies or intends either the deeds of the **Alban kings** <note>The legendary kings of Alba Longa, ancestors of the Romans.</note>—whose beginnings he abandoned because they were destroyed—or his early attempts at epic. Cynthian Apollo, named from Mount Cynthus in Delos where he was born, now wished to warn him to apply his ear <note>A famous image in the poem where Apollo pulls the poet's ear to remind him to stay humble.</note>. Therefore, the ear is stirred for the sake of memory, just as the forehead and face signify dignity.

It is noted that he was lead to sing a **fine-spun song** <note>original: "deductum... carmen"; a technical term in Roman poetics for a refined, slender, and highly polished style of poetry, as opposed to "fat" or "swollen" epic verse.</note>. "Fine-spun" refers to the thinnest thread which is drawn out into slenderness. The order of the text is: **"Now I will meditate on the rustic Muse on a slender reed"** <note>original: "Nunc ego agreste tenui meditabor harundine musam"; Eclogue 6.8.</note>. Here, before Varus, he lives on and even surpasses **Marius** <note>original: "marianum"; likely referring to the Roman general Gaius Marius.</note>, and brings glory through the wealth by which he conquers. He had remembered hearing of many sad wars—the "epithet of the spirit of wars."

# Bucolics.

<margin>Epicurus</margin>
And this same Epicurus, and those who follow him now, approve of none of these [previous theories], but they say that there are two principles of things: **body** and the **void**. Everything that exists either holds or is held. And again, they want these to be **atoms**, that is, as if the smallest parts which do not receive a "tome" <note>original: "thomi"; referring to the Greek *tomos*, meaning a cut or section.</note> or division. Whence they are called **atoms** because they are <unclear>indivisible</unclear>, and it is said there that they cannot cease to be divided. The **void** indeed they call the space in which the atoms exist.

<margin>Anaxagoras</margin>
Therefore, from these two principles, they claim these four are generated: **Fire**, **air**, **water**, and **earth**. And from these, all other things come. Those first two [body and void] are elements, but these four are <term>syntheta</term> <note>From the Greek *syntheta*, meaning "compounds" or things put together.</note>, that is, composed from those two preceding all other things. Reason proves that atoms and the void exist because there is nothing in the nature of things that does not also possess a body. And because it does not receive a division, it also introduces emptiness.

"For he sang," he says <note>original: "Ha manu p̄manē cauda fera canebat inquit"; the OCR is heavily corrupted here, but the commentator is quoting Virgil’s line: *Namque canebat uti magnum per inane coacta...* ("For he sang how, gathered through the great void...")</note>, that the beginning of the world is the space out of which, in great heat, the atoms had been [gathered] through the great void: all the seeds of fire, air, earth, and sea. For he called the atoms "seeds."

Now, they called this an "atom" <note>original: "atomus"; the text discusses the gender and definition of the word.</note> and this "atom" is a diminutive, because from it all things are come: the winds and the liquids together, the pure fire and the ether. He himself holds all things, the world having been led into a coinciding order of orbits, and thus all things that are in the world. For if the order were changed, or if all things were wings <note>The Latin here is likely a corruption of *penna* for *paene* (almost).</note>, they would have been collected and formed together in the world.

<margin>Heraclitus</margin>
Then at last the ground [began] to harden and to shut off the sea <note>original: "Tunc demum solum et discludere mea ponto"; a corruption of Virgil's line *Tum durare solum et discludere Nerea ponto*, referring to the separation of land and sea (represented by the sea-god Nereus).</note>...

# The Bucolics

They say [the poet tells you] to **move your feet** <note>A reference to the opening line of Eclogue 9: "Whither do your feet lead you, Moeris?"</note> in order to listen. And there is a **bud** <note>original: *gemma*; can mean a literal bud or a metaphorical jewel/eye of a vine</note> from those behind us while we think [of the past], and coming forward toward those things, it shows that for many people, the length of life is often a cause of misfortune <unclear>a</unclear>, because they are <unclear>changed</unclear>. This is because unexpected dangers are evil, wherefore he says: "A man says, 'I was able to hope for such great grief,'" and he says he can endure it if he survives. And it <unclear>can</unclear> be said that these victors do what they want, having imposed [their will] with equal **law** <unclear>jure</unclear>, since they cannot do what they want. Otherwise, those whom he conquered are miserable; they are "exchanged" because they persist in wars. **"Fortune turns all things"** <note>original: *fors omnia versat*; a famous line from Eclogue 9.5 regarding the unpredictability of fate</note>.

It should matter <unclear>nothing</unclear> to your person, just as it might bring back a hope <note>original: *aspe*; likely *aspero* (harsh) or *aspectu* (sight)</note> that has been described as narrow; all things are scholarly, all things are able to change from one state to another for those whom [fortune] turns well. Or else they drive toward the worse; he is conquered, and all this should be accepted as a matter of **mercy** <unclear>misericordie</unclear>.

Now, this is the example concerning **Hector and Ajax**:

Whence that <unclear>gift</unclear> <note>original: *exennium*; likely *xenium* (a guest-gift)</note> was born. **"The gods grant favor"** <note>original: *Dij bene uoltant*</note>, because what he **rules** <unclear>regit</unclear> is full of good things, but evil things are changed. From on high into the fields, it dissolves all the way to the water of the

# The Bucolics

<margin>Epirus</margin>
Menalcas <unclear>n</unclear> <unclear>vnu</unclear> <unclear>imgibus</unclear>, but **our songs** <note>original: *Carmina nra*; refers to Eclogue 9.11, where Lycidas notes that poetry has no power against the violence of war</note> have only so much strength among **martial weapons** <note>original: *mavortia tela*; Mars was the Roman god of war</note> [as doves do when the eagle comes]. He speaks of **Chaonian** <note>original: *Chaonias*; a reference to the Chaonians of Epirus, where the oracle of Dodona was located</note> birds, by which he means **doves** <note>original: *columbas*</note>. They provide omens and signs to the ancestors, nor are they of those <unclear>vium</unclear>, although he previously sought out the Chaonian ones.

In **Epirus** <note>A region in northwestern Greece</note>, it is said there was a grove in which doves gave responses [prophecies]. This is because in the **Thessalian language** <note>original: *lingua Thessala*</note>, the word ***peliades*** <note>From the Greek *peleiai*</note> refers both to "doves" and to "prophetesses." They are often [seen] before the tombs; it is pleasing to the great <unclear>Monae</unclear> in the **shadow** <note>original: *umbra*</note>.

If the **crow** <note>original: *cornix*</note> on the **left** <note>original: *sinistra*</note> had not warned him from the **hollow [oak]** <note>original: *caua*; referring to line 15: *ante sinistra cava monuisset ab ilice cornix*</note>, he would have departed. This crow belongs to the **augural discipline** <note>original: *augurale disciplina*</note>, for the augurs designate spaces in the open air, and thus they give measurements so that the part in front is called the **front** <note>original: *antica*</note>, the back is the **rear** <note>original: *postica*</note>, and then there is the **right** <note>original: *dextra*</note> and the **left** <note>original: *sinistra*</note>. Now, therefore, he says that the omens came from none of these [other] parts, but flew from the front toward the left side and settled in a **hollow** <note>original: *caua*</note> place, a thing which signifies a loss of **stars** <unclear>astrozu</unclear>.

The **holm-oak** <note>original: *Ilex*</note> is an **acorn-bearing tree** <note>original: *glandifera arbor*</note> which <unclear>qmy</unclear> is <unclear>vuoca</uncle>; it was not possible to hear the warning through the many shouts and <unclear>halaz</unclear>. But [the crow] was here before and was delighted by the noise. In other places, they frequently urge this; here, it is said the augurs abstain from the <unclear>onemofie</unclear> of the military, who are able to <unclear>possint</unclear> [be present] in **flourishing studies** <note>original: *virentibus studis*</note>.

Then the tyrant, moved—alas!—he falls, he says, because by his crimes and neglects he hears in his heart that he could have [succeeded]; he was frozen, as if stunned. "**While doing**" <note>original: *Inter agendum*; a reference to Eclogue 9.24: "Inter agendum, pasto, pascit ante, capellas" (While I am on my way, feed my goats)</note>—while I act. Now it is written with familiarity, through [various] words; again, let it be joined to new human things.
