<meta>This page marks the transition from Virgil's pastoral poetry (the Eclogues) to his didactic work on farming, the Georgics. The text serves as an "accessus" or formal introduction, identifying Virgil’s literary models—Homer, Theocritus, and Hesiod—and outlining the structure of the four books of the Georgics.</meta>

<header>The Beginning of the Georgics <note>original: *theorgicorum pring.*, likely an abbreviation for *Georgicorum principium*</note></header>

<margin>
Homer
Theocritus
Hesiod
</margin>

# Virgil in his works
followed various poets. He followed Homer in the *Aeneid*, though he followed him at a long interval <note>A common medieval sentiment that Virgil could never quite equal Homer's majesty</note>. In the *Bucolics*, he followed Theocritus, and is not far off from him. In these books [the *Georgics*], he followed Hesiod, whom he has left behind completely <note>original: *penitus reliquit*; this suggests that Virgil either moved beyond Hesiod's style or surpassed his model entirely</note>.

<margin>
The island of Ascra <note>The scribe identifies Ascra as an island, though it was actually a village in mainland Greece</note>
Perses
</margin>

Now, this Hesiod was from the island of Ascra. He wrote a book to his brother Perses which they call <term>erganemeras</term> <note>original: *Erga kai Hemerai*; Greek for "Works and Days"</note>, that is, "Works and Days." This book shows how and at what times the fields are to be cultivated. When, therefore, Virgil wished to transfer this to Latin, he established it just as he did with the *Bucolics*. Just as the *Aeneid* is named in imitation of the *Odyssey* and the <unclear>titles of other Greek works</unclear>. In the first book, he expresses the practice [of farming] through his words. In two [of the books], he describes what work and at what times the field must be cultivated. However, our poet indicated his greatness before this by compressing broad subjects and expanding narrower ones. For while Homer and Theocritus collected their writings in brevity, Virgil set aside Hesiod's book in a way that does not lack reason. For there, he teaches through the mouth of the earth itself, as if present.

<margin>
The Field:
1. Management <note>original: *Rationalis*</note>
2. Planted <note>original: *consitus*; referring to orchards and vineyards</note>
3. Pastoral <note>original: *pasturalis*; referring to livestock</note>
4. Flowery <note>original: *floreus*; referring to gardens and bees</note>
</margin>

He divides the work into four parts: for either it concerns the management of the fields <note>the "rational" part</note>, or the planting of trees and vines, or the pasturing of livestock (which is handled elsewhere), or the "flowery" part in the fourth book, which deals with bees and flowers. However, some wrongly assert that the *Georgics* consist of only two books, saying that <term>georgicam</term> <note>original: *πε' γεωργων* (peri georgon); Greek for "concerning farmers"</note> refers only to the act of farming.

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Virgil’s Georgics. While the previous page focused on the mythological and astronomical role of the moon and Proserpina, the text now shifts to a detailed etymological and historical explanation of the Roman calendar and the division of the year into months and seasons, likely providing context for the agricultural timing mentioned in Virgil's poem.</meta>

November <note>The text begins by discussing the placement of months in the ancient calendar</note>... it is especially corrected and shown that there were only ten months among the ancestors. For the ancestors, they first established this for **Mars** <note>March</note>, the author of their race. **April** is named, it is said, because it is the time when the season is "opening" <note>original: "aperturus"; a common ancient etymology deriving April from the Latin "aperire," to open, referring to budding flowers</note>.

**May** is named for the elders <note>original: "maioribus"</note>, and **June** from the juniors <note>original: "iunioribus"</note>; others say he <note>likely referring to Romulus or Numa Pompilius, legendary kings of Rome</note> wished these two months to be marked for the elders and the juniors because the Roman people had previously been divided into "centuries" of juniors and seniors. 

The remaining months were noted by number: **Quintilis** <note>the fifth month, now July</note>, **Sextilis** <note>the sixth month, now August</note>, **September** <note>the seventh</note>, **October** <note>the eighth</note>, **November** <note>the ninth</note>, and **December** <note>the tenth</note>. And these were the only ten months. Two more, however, were established following the signs of the heavens, which were later marked as **January** <note>from Janus</note> and **February**.

<margin>February</margin>
February is named from the "paternal Dis" <note>original: "ditis patr-"; referring to Dis Pater, the god of the underworld. February was a month of purification and sacrifices to the dead</note> to whom they sacrificed in that month. **Quintilis** and **Sextilis** were changed later in honor of Julius Caesar and Augustus; hence they are now **July** and **August**, as they stand in all the calendars <note>original: "fastis"</note>.

Therefore, regarding the new beginning of the year, all things are treated briefly. For the times of the year are divided among us, and the months make such a distinction of the seasons' progress: just as in the first month of **Spring**, it is a "new" leadership <note>the beginning of growth</note>; then Spring moves toward "adulthood" <note>full bloom</note>. In the same way, we see the "new" **Summer**, then its "adult" phase, or its ripening <note>original: "coctura," literally a "cooking" or ripening by the sun</note>, which is the final stage before the fall. **Winter** follows...

<meta>The previous page discussed the Roman calendar and the etymology of the months. This page transitions into a technical commentary on the sources Virgil used for his *Georgics* (a poem on farming), specifically referencing ancient authorities on agriculture and providing practical instructions for plowing based on soil type and season.</meta>

<margin>Xenophon</margin>
It is certainly worth knowing that **Xenophon** <note>A Greek philosopher and historian (c. 430–354 BCE)</note> wrote two books of the *Oeconomicus* <term>Oeconomicus: a Greek treatise on household management and agriculture</term>. The first part of this work is entirely concerned with agriculture; in the second part, **Virgil** transferred many things to this present work. **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture</note> also brings in matters <margin>Mago</margin> from the *Georgics* of **Mago** <note>Mago the Carthaginian, known as the "father of agriculture" for his 28-volume manual</note>.

**Marcus Terentius Varro** <note>An influential Roman scholar (116–27 BCE) who wrote "De Re Rustica"</note> says in his first book of the *Oeconomicus* what pertains to agriculture; for the first precept here is how the **mother of the household** <note>original: "mater familias"</note> ought to conduct herself at home. The second is how she should manage matters in public <note>original: "forensem"</note>. It should also be known that in these books there is no mixture of obstacles or digressions through questions, as there is in the *Aeneid*, which is quite extensive. But in this work, there is only a difficulty in understanding through the poets, which is <term>poikilon</term> <note>original: ΠΟΙΚΙΛΟΝ; Greek for "varied" or "intricate," referring to the complex literary style of the work</note>.

There are three primary precepts signified here. For he says that a **fertile**, rich, and grassy field ought to be plowed in the **spring**. It should be plowed once in the springtime so that weeds may be pulled up at that time <note>original: "ad tenorem"</note> before they go to seed, and so that the superfluous moisture may be dried out by the heat of summer, or so that the hardness of the clods may soften. Once a field is plowed with seeds <note>likely referring to the preparation for sowing</note>, a **thin and sterile** field should instead be plowed toward the **autumn** season. This is so that if the same field were plowed in the spring, the summer drought would snatch away its moisture.

Namely, let the white snows be dissolved into water <note>A reference to Virgil’s "Georgics" 1.43: "vere novo, gelidus canis cum montibus umor liquitur"</note>.
<margin>Liquor</margin>
**Liquor** <note>original: "liquor / oris"</note> is a noun here; the vowel is short, whereas when it is produced from the verb "liquitur" <note>to melt or flow</note>, it is long, as in "the liquid rests" <unclear>...</unclear>

<margin>in vain</margin>

Where there is something poorly [placed] in a passage, they read it as: "the Father [Jupiter] is present on the earth," lest he strike in vain.

For P. <note>likely referring to the poet Publius Vergilius Maro or a commentator like Probus</note> says from here: see that he strikes you as **gloomy** <note>original: *tristem*</note> and strikes [you], which can hardly proceed. <margin>two solstices</margin>

Hence the days of the winter solstice are less—the shortest—and the summer ones are the longest while they last.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Virgil’s Georgics, specifically addressing Book 1, line 100: "Pray for moist solstices and clear winters." The text moves from the poet's specific advice to a broader explanation of the four points of the year—solstices and equinoxes—and the use of poetic license in Virgil's grammar.</meta>

<margin>Equinox</margin>
Virgil <note>original: *Maro*; the family name of the poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> says, therefore, that farmers ought to pray for rains during the **solstices** and for clear skies during the **winter**. As we have said, it is good when the heat is favorable, even leading up to the winter solstice.

But first, remember the components and the division: there are two solstices and two equinoxes. One is the **vernal** (spring) equinox and the other is the **autumnal** equinox, which the Greeks call <term>isēmerias</term> <note>original: *ισημεριασ*; meaning "equal days," referring to the time when day and night are of equal length</note>. These occur on the eighth day before the Kalends of April <note>March 25</note> and the eighth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 24</note>.

This is because, in the ancient past, the year was divided into only two parts: **winter** and **summer**. The winter solstice is what divides the two hemispheres, for he wishes the appearance of all the seasons to be fulfilled. For he says from this that it is to be hoped that, just as there should be clear weather in the autumn and winter seasons—because two <unclear>extra</unclear> seasons will be counted as one according to the logic of the cycle—so too in the spring and summer seasons there should be rains, since those seasons will also be counted as one.

But if one attends to the text carefully, there is a use of **poetic license** <note>original: *poetica licentia*; the liberty taken by a poet to ignore strict rules of grammar or fact for the sake of the verse</note> where he uses the plural number in place of the singular. For he wrote "**solstices**" instead of "solstice" and "**winters**" instead of "winter." 

He says these conditions are to be prayed for because they do not happen by nature alone, so that the harshness of both seasons might be softened: in the summer, the heat is tempered by rain; and in the cold of winter, by clear weather. During the winter time, the **winter dust** <note>Referring to Virgil's claim that "winter dust" (*hiberno pulvere*) brings great joy to the crops</note> and winter clarity are beneficial because they keep things clean...

<summary>This page explains Virgil's agricultural advice regarding weather, detailing the Roman dates for equinoxes and explaining the poet's use of plural nouns as "poetic license." It highlights the ancient division of the year into two primary seasons and the benefits of atypical weather for crop health.</summary>

<keywords>Virgil, Georgics, solstice, equinox, poetic license, Roman calendar, agriculture, meteorology, March 25, September 24</keywords>

Hence it is natural and possible by its own indication <note>original: *indicio*</note> that they can be either joyful or sad. These things could not happen in any other way unless they follow the act of nature itself, and according to its quality, they appear either joyful or sad. Nor does the air seem to foretell things by its own nature, but rather things follow it as they are drawn toward either favorable or adverse conditions.

But we, even among the clouds, are able to be joyful in a skillful serenity of things <note>A reference to human reason and the ability to remain "tranquil" even in bad weather, unlike animals who are physically affected by the atmosphere.</note> through fate and prudence. Virgil uses the metaphor of a ship beginning its voyage to describe the start of his poem.</note> as if flying; grant favor to these simple and other poems <term>songs</term> <note>original: *carmina*. Here, he himself ensures the song is easy beforehand by saying: **"In hand are the lands"** <note>original: *In manibus terre*. From *Georgics* 2.45. It implies that the subject matter is "at hand" or "within reach," not distant or unreachable.</note>; this is easy and ready where the gate is. 

And **"I do not wish to embrace all things"** <note>original: *non ego cuncta moror amplecti opto*. From *Georgics* 2.42. Virgil is stating that he will not cover every single detail of agriculture, but will pick the most beautiful and relevant parts.</note>, that is, I am not sent away; it is said whether I can narrate, and he expresses his devotion and his ability; and I shall deserve [praise] from all his songs which are briefly charming. 

Others understand this because it is established that **Maro** <note>Virgil's full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> was born skilled in letters and composed many poems. For he even described the deeds and accomplishments of **Augustus**, which Horace testifies to when he says: 

**"You yourself [Maecenas] will better tell of Caesar’s battles in prose histories, and of the necks of threatening kings led through the streets"** <note>original: *Tu quoque pedestribus... historiis proelia Caesaris...*. A reference to Horace, *Odes* 2.12.9-12. Horace suggests that Maecenas is better suited to write a prose history of Augustus (Caesar), while the poets handle the verse.</note>. 

And he wants this to be said: "Be present together with the undertaken labor and devotedly"; and at the same time I shall write... also that in histories it is established that there are talents; but my song will be made brief, and let it all be that [descriptive] epithet.

# On the Labors of the Seasons

The bold and sharp [season] <note>original: *improbus acer*; likely referring to the onset of winter or the relentless nature of agricultural labor, a common theme in Virgil (cf. *labor omnia vicit improbus*).</note> is to be feared in its own manner; then the brevity of the rains deceives and frustrates the labor. There are no vegetables, nor any others—they gather none, that is, only some. Not even in the vineyards do the fruits <note>original: *poma*; specifically orchard fruits or any fruit-bearing tree.</note> await the **pruning hook** <gloss>curved blade</gloss> to be pruned, which however he refers to the industry at the edge [of the field]. For even now, the duties require care... <unclear>aniare</unclear>... the pits of the furrows are properly for March <note>original: *Marti*; the month of March was the traditional time for heavier spring plowing and trenching.</note>. Poured forth more excessively with moisture, it provides for the trees. When it pours out the thongs from its own **breast** <gloss>heart</gloss>, so much, that is, from its own heart. # On the Utility of Wild Trees

With all good things—that is, immediately through prayer—namely these things, of these, etc. It is announced, however, through many ways, for through the act itself, because they can be spread. With **waving boxwood** <note>original: *undante buxo*; Virgil’s poetic description of the shimmering leaves of boxwood trees.</note> on the mountain of **Cytorus** <note>A mountain in Paphlagonia (modern Turkey) renowned for its high-quality boxwood.</note>, in which boxwood abounds, which is moved by the wind or imitates the waves of the sea. # On the Uses of Forest Trees

Of the trees here from the forests, namely, for they [need] no [human help], and with pressure he produces wheels or spokes to be turned by the **lathe** <gloss>a machine for shaping wood</gloss>. They have fashioned solid wheels for wagons and for the roofs of vehicles, and curved **hulls** <note>original: *carinas*; literally the "keels" or bodies of ships.</note>. But on the other hand, in other places, myrtles are used for strong **spear-shafts** <note>original: *hastilibus*</note> and for the shepherd’s goad with its pressed point, and the **dogwood** <note>original: *cornus*; the cornelian cherry tree, known for its extremely hard wood.</note> is good for war. Indeed, their dogwood is suitable for shafts of both kinds, and for the likeness of **Ituraean bows** <note>original: *iturorum arcum*; the Ituraeans of the Levant were celebrated in antiquity as expert archers.</note>. Nor do the smooth **linden trees** <note>original: *l[ine]e*; referring to *tiliae*</note> and the boxwood lack their place; they receive their form from the lathe. 

There is also the wood sent down the **Po** <note>The Po River in northern Italy, used for transporting timber.</note>; there is hope for the species of wood which is more rare in other forests. He also wants more of the decaying trees; from here they drink the water. We call it "hollow" <note>original: *alvum*; likely referring to hollowed-out trunks used for beehives or small boats.</note> for the sake of the **river** <note>original: *fuvessum*; likely a corruption of *fluvium*</note>.

-> **O too fortunate...** <-

**O too fortunate [farmers], if they but knew their own blessings!** <note>Refers to Virgil’s famous line: *O fortunatos nimium, sua si bona norint, agricolas*.</note> This is an abrupt transition to the praise of the rustic life. Thus, even in the praise of the countryside, he not only praises the life of justice but also its gratitude...

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
In the temple, because he wished even him to rejoice, he might sound forth praises for this man.
Regarding the term **unpraised** <note>original: *illaudati*; referring to the Egyptian tyrant Busiris mentioned in *Georgics* 3.4</note>, it is a figure of speech <note>likely *parhorie*, a corruption of *paroemia* or a similar rhetorical term</note> because it is used as **unpraisable**. It does not refer to someone who is not praised because he does not exist, but to one who does not deserve to be praised. This is like that phrase in the book of <note>OCR: *lio: kat. entut. diurio*; likely a corrupt reference to a legal or grammatical text</note> regarding the word **inaccessible**: it refers not to those whom no one has reached, but to those whom no one *should* approach. Of whom does **Greece** <note>original: *Hellas*; though in the context of Virgil's poem, this often introduces the story of Hylas</note> not speak? 

<margin>Hylas. Horace.</margin>
The boy <note>original: *puer*; referring to Hylas, the companion of Hercules</note>, that is, the one from the water. **Horace** [writes] in his books... <note>The text here appears to be a fragmented reference to Hylas being lost to the water nymphs</note>. Moreover, in the story of **Hylas**, **Hercules** was the first who acted... <note>OCR: *pfetas naplus*; possibly referring to his search for the boy</note>.

<margin>Latona. Delos. Apollo. Diana.</margin>
Regarding **Latona**, **Delos** is the island in which she gave birth to **Apollo** and **Diana**. This island was once wandering, but Apollo [made it stationary], as we read in the *Prologue* <note>or perhaps the *Georgics* or *Aeneid*</note>, it is high and moved... <note>OCR: *muono e celsa*; likely *immota et celsa* (unmoved and high)</note>. We shall speak more fully of this fable in its proper place.

<margin>Hippodamia.</margin>
**Hippodamia** is a Greek name... <note>The text discusses the name's variations</note> which is changed by men themselves in our language so that it is said as **Hippodame**, **Hippodamia**, or like **Penelope** and **Penelopia**. The story is as follows: **Hippodamia**

<margin>Oenomaus.</margin>
was the daughter of **Oenomaus**, the king of Elis and Pisa. This man had horses that were the swiftest of all, descended from the winds <note>original: *nepote ventorum*</note>. Because of his daughter, he challenged many who came to a contest under this condition: that either he, if defeated, would hand over his daughter, or he would kill those he defeated.

<margin>Pelops. Myrtilus.</margin>
Afterward, when she had fallen in love with **Pelops**, **Hippodamia** corrupted **Myrtilus**, the charioteer, having first made certain agreements. This having been done, [he tampered with] the wheels and axles, so that **Pelops** emerged as the victor and could possess the promised girl.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 4 of Virgil’s Georgics. Following the discussion of the bees' labor and social structure, the author now addresses the philosophical claim that bees possess a spark of the divine mind (the "divine breath"), comparing their physical and spiritual makeup to that of humans and the four classical elements.</meta>

Indeed, it is a glorious thing that drew them into the service of the king <note>original: "regis in stipendia traxit"; Virgil refers to the leader of the hive as a "rex" (king), though we now know it is a queen</note>, or here he speaks of the uprightness of men in their custom, as we read in Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian often cited for his moral and political commentary</note>, where one devotes himself with words so that they might refute [fate] with their lives. Concerning this [king] whom we rule, and these examples from his own mind... 

The commentary of this is full; he follows it in the book because he briefly connects them in this place so that, through Virgil, the bees might be seen to **have a share of divinity** <note>original: "apes partem habere divinitatis"; a reference to Georgics 4.221</note>. For it is manifest that all other things consist of the **four elements** <note>The classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire</note> and the divine spirit.

For they draw their flesh from the earth, moisture from the water, their breath from the air, and their heat from fire; but from the divine spirit they draw their character <note>original: "ingenium"</note>, which is **industry** in bees and [reason] in men. For they fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice <note>These are the four Stoic passions (metus, cupiditas, aegritudo, gaudium) which were thought to affect all living souls</note>, because many more things are condemned by those who are wise. Indeed, they gather flowers; they feel shame... 

Let us truly confess that even the bees have a share of divinity. So that he might adapt these ideas with examples in similar matters, he is fertile in argument when he speaks of those things which we cannot prove to have existed. From similar things that must be proven; for he teaches that the wind is corporeal <note>Having a physical body or substance</note>, not because we can hold or see it, but because its effect is recognized before its physical nature is known. It is manifest: the drafts and divine breaths. For we know by our own reason that a man is made in a body, having inspected the heaven and the earth and other things. He says the spirit is less... the gap in its own [place] that you ever see moved...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Virgil’s Georgics, Book 4. Having established that bees—and by extension, all living things—possess a "divine breath," the author now explores the transition of life back into the divine source, arguing that what we call "death" is merely a transformation or "resolution" of the elements into their original state.</meta>

From this source, all things go forth and emerge, and they live by the **divine spirit** <note>original: "divino spiritu"</note> once they have received life through birth. Moreover, as we have said, all things are composed of the elements; and so from this source, everything is undoubtedly returned, dissolved, and led back again into its origin. Nor is there any place for **death** <note>original: "morti"; the author argues here that in a universe of divine conservation, nothing truly ceases to exist</note> in the natural order, for there is nothing that can utterly perish. All things are returned in a state of resolution.

This phenomenon, however, which is called death, is not truly death, because it causes nothing to perish; rather, it is called **resolution** <note>original: "resolutio"; a technical term for the breaking down of a compound into its constituent parts</note>. Many now say that this is a "boundary" <note>original: "ora"; meaning a border or shore</note>, because it involves the breaking of the physical instrument and the dissolving of its connection. On the contrary, it is an honor to return to that which was before, leaving behind a narrow seat—that is, a place of safety. In its proper sense, "narrow" <note>original: "angustum"</note> is used for the **august** <note>original: "augusto"; the author is making a wordplay between "narrow/constrained" and "majestic/holy"</note>, a word generally used for what is noble and full of majesty. 

It is a treasury of things stored away; or perhaps it should be called **apotheosis** <term>Apotheosis: The process of becoming divine or being elevated to the status of a god</term>, which implies a "scattering." This is a participle used for a participle: "by the mouth of the shrine" <note>original: "ore fani"; this is likely a corruption of "Orpheus," the mythical musician who features at the end of Georgics 4</note>, he is drawn in by the scattering of water. One might invite them with a feather, or even prefer smoke; by these means, even in the depths of the underworld <note>original: "Helle"; likely a reference to the journey of Orpheus to reclaim Eurydice from the land of the dead</note>, he will be able to collect the honey himself. 

Others read "mouth of the shrine" <note>original: "ore fani"</note> so that it is as if it appears in the fifth [book?], or "by the mouth of the speaker." Let all follow the smoke of this holy one, as followers of the bees, so that they do not follow them in a base way.

<summary>This page presents a Neoplatonic interpretation of Virgil, arguing that death is merely the "resolution" of the body back into the elements and the divine spirit. It concludes with a mystical or allegorical reference to Orpheus and the collection of honey as a spiritual pursuit.</summary>
<keywords>death vs resolution, divine spirit, elements, august, apotheosis, Orpheus, bees, honey, Virgil</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 4 of Virgil’s *Georgics*. While the previous page dealt with the metaphysical "divine breath" and the nature of life and death, the author here transitions into the practical and astronomical signs governing the honey harvest, specifically interpreting Virgil's references to the stars and the behavior of the bees themselves.</meta>

Among the **Indians** <note>original: "Indis"; Virgil suggests that in warmer climates like India, nature is even more prolific</note>. Because they drive forth great offspring, the fertility of honey is at its peak. There are **two times for the harvest** <note>original: "duo tempora messis"</note>: that is, in the spring during June, and again when one might now take the harvest <note>original: "deprehendere messem"</note>.

Touching upon the stars: **Taygete** <note>original: "Taygete"; one of the seven stars of the Pleiades constellation</note> is one of the **Pleiades** <note>original: "pleiadibz"</note>. As we have said twice before, honey must be collected twice: first at the rising of the Pleiades (that is, in the spring) and second when they set in the autumn season. 

It encounters the rivers. To man, these are sweet, or rather, in the manner of a flowing stream, its currents are destined to return. Whether poor or the same, the **constellation of the Fish** <note>original: "sidus... piscis"; referring to the constellation Pisces or the sun's position relative to water-bearing signs</note> brings the winter waters. But he who looks up at the water from the mouth of **Aquarius** <note>original: "aquarii" — the Water-Bearer</note>, where he also added the lambs to yours, is thus called the Fish. At this time, the season is more sorrowful, either because of the setting of the sun or because of the proximity of winter's harshness. 

Their anger is beyond measure <note>original: "praemodum supra est"</note>; they exceed all bounds. For when they are provoked, they engage in battle among themselves. They place their short **stings** <term>Spicula: The barbed sting of a bee, which Virgil famously noted remains in the victim at the cost of the bee's own life</term> in the wax, where they can hide in the wound. They do not do this out of their own nature, but because of an injury inflicted upon them. 

And it is said ambiguously that when you would hasten the smoke of your fires, which he was applying—namely, he was applying the stronger ones. By a **broken dismissal** <note>original: "missabe fractas"; likely referring to the dispersal of the swarm or the scent</note>, that is, by those things breathed upon them. **To fumigate with thyme** <note>original: "suffire timo fumigare"</note> so that other things mixed with them might flee, and to cut back the **empty waxes** <note>original: "cerasqz recidere inanes"</note>. Truly, they say this if they have nothing left in the hives, either because you have taken it or because the previous inhabitants have consumed it.

It also discusses the defensive behavior of bees (their stings) and the necessity of fumigating hives with thyme to manage the colony.</summary>

<meta>This page marks a significant transition in the manuscript. Having concluded the commentary on Virgil’s *Georgics* on the previous page, the scribe now begins a new work: *De Deo Socratis* (On the God of Socrates) by the 2nd-century North African philosopher and orator, Apuleius of Madaurus. This text is a famous defense of Socratic philosophy and a treatise on the nature of "daemons" or intermediary spirits.</meta>

## Apuleius the Platonic philosopher of Madaurus
### The book on the God of Socrates begins;

**Y**ou who have wished for me to speak, I now receive this first trial <note>original: "rudimentum," meaning a beginning or initial attempt</note> after experience. Indeed (as is my opinion) I shall make a trial with a "good risk," since I am about to speak more pleasant, meditated things among you. For I do not fear that among those studious of learning, the discipline which has pleased in my orations [will be lacking]. His manifold provision, even in this (as Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the Roman satirist</note> says) **extemporaneous sketch** <note>original: "schedio," referring to an informal or impromptu composition</note>, strives to put itself to the same test of its own in that which is premeditated.
<margin>otherwise: the very same</margin> Just as our sudden glance recognizes a very well-known face, so certainly you may suffer the labor of listening to that which we write, which we bestow upon you more readily. For thus affection is confessed among you wise ones; in premeditated works, there is deliberation, meditation, and instruction; but in sudden matters, there is a more generous indulgence. For written things are weighed and examined, but sudden things [are accepted] I know not how, at once. And not without cause. For he who speaks written things transmits to us such things as were brought in <note>i.e., prepared beforehand</note>. But he who provides [sudden words] suffers such things as are to be shared with us, or such as **Fortune** <note>the goddess of chance</note> makes for you in the doing. Concerning this, I shall be moderated for you in order, so that you may hear my arrival gladly. It is placed in your hand or by your power <note>original: "numere," likely a scribal error for "munere" (gift/duty)</note> that you now send them forth, not as things hanging and flaccid, nor as if obstructed and brought back. Of this, I find nearly everything under those auspices of which **Aristippus** <note>A follower of Socrates and founder of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy</note> spoke. And what, by Hercules, was said by that disciple of Socrates, when a certain tyrant asked him what the study of philosophy had cost him and what he had gained from it. He answered justly: "so that he might converse with all men without fear" <note>This is a famous anecdote illustrating the confidence philosophy provides in social and political life</note>. This sentiment was taken up by a sudden word because it arose from the unexpected, just as when a stone from the sea reaches land, he places it in its time.

<summary>This page serves as the prologue to Apuleius's "On the God of Socrates," where the author discusses the difference between prepared speeches and impromptu oratory, citing the philosopher Aristippus.</summary>
<keywords>Apuleius, Socrates, Aristippus, philosophy, oratory, Lucilius, extemporaneous speech, fortune</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Apuleius’s prologue to *De Deo Socratis*. Following the previous page’s discussion on the "extemporaneous sketch," the author here contrasts the craftsmanship of a polished, written speech with the dangers of speaking "from the moment." He uses architectural metaphors and Aesop’s fables to illustrate the risks of seeking quick praise at the expense of careful preparation.</meta>

<margin>the envious one</margin>

Neither does thinness weigh down the reckless, nor does the aiming [of the eye] serve as the frontispiece <note>likely referring to the decorative facade of a building or a speech</note>. Nor is it done by simply adding line upon line; for if an oration is constructed on both sides—the one currently being handled—it is no less drawn from mountain stone <note>suggesting the heavy, durable quality of a well-crafted speech</note>. I might have learned my duty properly, as an explained and lighter work, with the best edges leveled **to the nail** <term>to the nail (ad unguem): a sculptor’s term for testing the smoothness of a joint with one's fingernail; it means "perfectly finished"</term>. If anyone should build a work with either rough inequality, or slippery thresholds, or clashing angles, or rolling rounds without the correction of a rule, and a small amount of measure, and the skill of the plumb line; no matter can be produced from that same thing which is at once both hurried and examined.

Nor is it a joke that you can have both the praise of diligence and the grace of speed at the same time. A certain wish was offered to me (and it was greatly desired by me) that I should speak **extemporaneously** <note>original: "ex tempore," meaning "out of the moment" or without preparation</note>. This is a pervasive fear: lest that should happen to me which **Aesop** sang in his fables regarding his crow. For that bird, gaping for praise, lost the part he had taken before, having been captured by a new part.

If you ask about the **moral story** <term>apologue (apologus): a moral fable, especially one involving animals</term>: it will not be a burden to tell another fable. A crow and a fox had seen a single little bone at the same time. And because it was hurried by a seizure of equal zeal, with force and speed—the fox by running, the crow by flying—the winged beast had already arrived first. Gliding ahead with a second flight, with wings spread on both sides, he anticipated [the fox]. And thus, happy with both the prey and the victory, he escaped on high and sat safe in the topmost summit of a nearby oak tree. Afterward, the fox, who did not know the "wing-footed" <note>original: "alipedem," often referring to Mercury or swift creatures; here mocking the fox's lack of wings</note> tricks of the bird, followed to the same tree. Standing below, when he saw the predator above exulting in his prey, he began to praise him with cunning: "Indeed, I thought such beauty was sought elsewhere from **Apollo** <note>The god of prophecy and music, often associated with beauty and ravens/crows</note> in vain; but here I see the physical prize? Truly, I must pray for it, though it is small; but as far as use is concerned, how soft the plumage, how sharp the head..."

<vocab>Aesop, fable, crow, fox, apologue, to the nail, oration, tricks</vocab>

<summary>Apuleius uses the metaphor of a master stonemason to describe the difficulty of balancing speed and precision in oratory, concluding with an Aesopic fable about a crow's vanity to warn against the dangers of seeking "extemporaneous" praise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the prologue to Apuleius's *De Deo Socratis*. Following the previous page's mention of Aesop’s fable of the crow, the author now elaborates on the symbolic colors of the bird and the trickery of the fox to illustrate the dangers of vanity in speech. He then transitions into a justification for translating his philosophical thoughts from Greek into Latin.</meta>

his beak was strong. Now you may see it for yourself with your own eyes. By great commands <note>original: "praecep," likely *praeceptis*</note>. For let me say this regarding color: since two colors were most excellent—pitch-black and snow-white—they were not so distant from one another. Apollo <note>The god of music and prophecy, often associated with the swan (white) and the raven (black)</note> bestowed both colors upon his own limbs: I travel through the white color in **meter** <note>poetic verse</note>; but the pitch-black one he drew forth with a dark **song**; so he devoted himself to this. Nor will he stand out so much publicly elsewhere as he will among friends, far surpassing good men by seeing the madness of the hungry while the Muse held the tongue.

But when that [shrewd fox] <note>The OCR "conius" likely refers to the fox (vulpes) in the fable</note> heard that only this [a voice] was missing from him: he wanted that clearest sound so that he would not appear to have been given a false gift. Forgotten of the duty <note>original: "officii," referring to the crow's task of holding the food</note> which he was holding in his bite, he gaped with his whole mouth <note>original: "toto rictu gyanit," likely *hianit* (gaped)</note>. And so, what he had produced by gnawing, he lost the cheese <note>original: "canem" is likely a transcription error for *caseum* (cheese), following the Aesop fable</note>; it is a common story that what he had lost by effort, they recovered by craft.

Finally, the fable itself is condensed into a few words? Because then he was restrained from acting. And of those, as if a vocal performance were pleasing, that which alone was missing—and for the sake of simulated beauty—the **Greek** <term>Greek (Graecus): referring here to the Greek language or a Greek-style rhetorical approach</term> version arrives, which was suitable in its mouth for a reply as it was once before. This is a clear case of the change, so that they might follow the path into **Latin** <term>Latin (Latine): the language of the Roman people, which Apuleius is now employing for his audience</term>. For even in the beginning, he returned different things to you: so I remember promising that neither would be purely lacking, neither what is Greek nor what is Latin would be entirely cut off <note>original: "dichome," likely referring to a dichotomy or division</note> from this departure.

Therefore (if it seems so), I truly pray for your [attention]. It is time to migrate into Latin from Greek; for since these things come from a middle ground, so that (which is your opinion) this later version might not be for that little speech <note>original: "oretta," perhaps a diminutive for a speech or prayer</note> which he spoke before, nor be inferior in arguments, nor lesser in thoughts, nor poor in examples, nor dissonant in speech; but even more full of substance. Which especially pertains to the hearing... [he] dared because from the smoke of the day, smoke, a nest, and an isthmus; make it so you understand. Not only with a dissolution, but...

<meta>This page transitions from the introductory fables (the crow and the fox) to the core philosophical treatise of *De Deo Socratis*. # The Nature of the Visible Gods

...is it not even worthy? These things are also [granted] to me by more than one master, just as if they were many. He makes the order more manifest from the arrangement of their place. For just as majesty requires, among mortal masters some are enriched [with status]. Those celestial gods whom we partially claim by sight, and others whom we suspect in that light; not by carnal sight alone.

> O you most brilliant lights of the world, gliding through the sky, who lead the year. <note>original: "o clarissima mundi lumina labentia caelo q’ ducitis annū." A quotation from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book 1, lines 5-6), referring to the Sun and Moon.</note>

Nor [should we overlook] in that special creation of the divine Artisan <note>original: "opificis," referring to the Creator or Demiurge</note> the moon, which is the rival of the sun and mistress of the night, whether she be horned <note>crescent</note>, or swollen <note>gibbous</note>, or full, she changes her face. She acts appropriately as she is illuminated by the sun, the further she moves away from it, through the increases of her phases and light.

<margin>Enduringly.</margin>
She dispenses the months by her own increases and the successions of days. Whether she shines with her own brightness—as the Chaldaeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers famous for their planetary observations</note> think—being possessed of light in one part, but empty of brightness in the other: according to the motion of her rotation, she changes her appearance by showing her illuminated face. Or whether she is entirely lacking in her own brightness and stands in need of light from elsewhere, [receiving] the heat of the moon or a certain scattering of rays.

<margin>Our [light], i.e., borrowed. <note>original: "adulterinā" (adulterine), used here in the sense of 'not original' or 'counterfeit' light borrowed from the sun.</note></margin>
By the opposition or the facing of the sun [she shines]. And as the poet <note>The transcription "barbi’ btar" likely refers to Lucretius (*De Rerum Natura*), whom Apuleius often cites regarding the moon's light.</note> said, "they cast night-light from their body." For I see this possibility. And it has taught me more about the moon than the sun in their specific steps... Nor regarding those, as I said, stars which are commonly called "wandering" <note>original: "vago," referring to the planets (from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning 'wanderer')</note> from their motion.

Yet, despite that flow, they display the most orderly journeys in divine successions by a certain and steady course; varying because of the spaces of their orbits, but always remaining one and equal, they simulate now progress and now retreat <note>A reference to retrograde motion, where planets appear to move backward in the sky</note> in a marvelous change. This depends on their position and curvature and the absence of their motions, which he who is well-skilled [in astronomy] knows are tempered according to the order of the zodiac signs. In that same number of visible gods are the other stars which were marked out at the first placement of the [divine] decree...

# The Choir of the Stars and the Twelve Gods

...radiating, those gods whom others see as a gathered and crowned choir <note>original: "chorum coactum," referring to the constellations</note> in the clear weather of painted nights. Let us look up with reverence to these gods. In this most perfect [gift] of the world, as Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), a foundational Roman poet often cited by later writers</note> says, there is a refined flame varied with brightness.

<margin>
Or: for duty <note>original: "l' pro munere"</note>
Truly it is moved by few <note>original: "r' ẽ ĩmoũt' pauciõb"</note>
Ruler of all things as well <note>original: "oim qq rerũ d̃nator"</note>
</margin>

There is another kind of gods, which Nature has denied to our sight, but whom we contemplate in wonder with the sharp edge of the mind <note>original: "aciem mentis," meaning intellectual intuition</note>, perceiving the god through the plant <note>or "foundation"</note>. Among those in the world, there are those twelve in number whose names were compressed into two verses by Ennius:

->**Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus,**<-
->**Mars, Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Apollo.**<-
<note>Ennius’s famous mnemonic list for the *Dii Consentes*, the twelve major deities of the Roman pantheon. Note that the transcription here omits Vulcan to fit the rhythm.</note>

And is this not their kind? Since the same thing is known by many gifts through long-recognized causes, they have divided the power of the divine through various utilities into a triple arrangement. There are three regions <note>traditionally Heaven, Sea, and Earth</note> which each of them protects. Others, through a misguided sense of reason, or perhaps through religious effort, have established the most solemn gods of the countryside through the most sacrilegious cult of Venus; part of them are swollen with superstition, and part with contempt.

For they place these gods in the heights, far removed from human contagion <note>original: "humana contagione," the idea that the supreme gods cannot be touched by the "pollution" of mortal life</note>. If they do not benefit all things, if they fear the merits of the impious, if they define the impure—these gods clearly consist of temporal natures. But if they wish to return to their beginning, if their bodies run forward and backward, they will change the penalty of their station. To a tyrant, who prepares no good for anyone else, the supreme beatitude <note>original: "summam beatitudinem"</note> is only his own, if indeed these things are good for him.

And to all things, the divine is continually ready, easy, simple, free, and absolute. Their merit is released from all times of doing something for the sake of the administration and adoration of all things; in no way is the path to the duties of the other gods obstructed. To whom, therefore, does this now apply, of whom Plato and other eloquent wise men dispute concerning the immortal gods? Most frequently he [Plato] comes forward...

<meta>This page continues the translation of Apuleius’s *De Deo Socratis* (On the God of Socrates). Having established the hierarchy of the visible and invisible celestial gods, the text now transitions into a philosophical meditation on the nature of divine majesty and the profound distance between the immortal gods and mortal humans.</meta>

# The Nature of Divine Majesty and the Human Condition

...of a majesty so incredible in its immensity and so ineffable that it cannot be fully captured in speech, nor can it be grasped even slightly except by the divine sages <note>original: "sapientibus divinis"</note>. To this vigor and more blessed state, the approach of the stars leads from this place; if any are bound by the tightest bonds of the swiftest white light <note>original: "lumine candido"</note> to reach the end. Therefore, having sent these things forth, I will make this the place [of my argument]. 

Yet, it is not so much for my own pleasure that I applaud those words where I may act for the gods above, where I have emerged into the world in long successions, so that I may move the same reasoning regarding the true nature of God. Indeed, they are in their own honors <note>original: "in propriis... honore"</note>. Because the custom of discipline is taught through paths that are distracted by unique and external origins, but we must grant our prayers and always the divine touch of his love, moved by his hand, so that no honor may seem to be lost to posterity. This is not due to a disparity of error if the divine distributes a difference to our own. 

Therefore, by this reasoning, we praise with pale faces <note>original: "ore pallente," suggesting the awe or frailty of the living</note>, with immortal souls <note>original: "immortalibus animis"</note>, but with diseased nourishment and languid limbs of the body <note>original: "leumbibus e corpore membris"</note>. And now, from these long bodies comes a most dissimilar disease. With similar errors, there is a meager authority, a vain hope, a hollow labor <note>original: "casso labore"</note>, and a falling fortune <note>original: "fortuna cadura"</note>. 

Of matching mortals, certain in all things which first affected the human race, we must suffice for that wonderful volume of time, with wisdom slow in its motion. Because your nature was unfolded, holding the earth, called by men the first place of boundaries and sublimity, no one is superior, and it is said that no day is truly one’s own. The highest desire of the passions is arranged there, living and nourishing, and because of this, these things are fleeting and very flowing. And while those things have been raised to blessedness <note>original: "beatitudinem"</note>, these here have been cast down to miseries. Therefore, no ignorance exists in the divine and spiritual part, even if the interrupted beast has suffered weakness. For as the divine Plato <note>The Greek philosopher Plato, whom Apuleius followed as a Middle Platonist</note> says: "No god mixes [directly] with men" <note>original: "nullu quid i miserat," a corruption of the famous Platonic dictum "nullus deus miscetur hominibus" from the *Symposium*</note>.

<summary>This page explores the vast ontological gap between the ineffable majesty of the immortal gods and the fragile, "diseased" condition of mortal humans, concluding with Plato's assertion that gods do not directly mingle with humanity.</summary>

# The Invisible Architect and the Majesty of the Divine

...[it] is awe-inspiring. And this small whole is a specimen of their sublimity <note>original: "sublimitatum sperman," likely a corruption of *sublimatum specimen*</note>, such that no hand of an architect <note>original: "architectata manu"</note> has contaminated any part of them. They seem to hold onto only as much as is intended to be made. Regarding their appearance, size, and colors <note>original: "odoribus," though context in Apuleius's *De Deo Socratis* usually refers to the visual appearance and qualities of the divine</note>, there is still debate. Yet their excellence is perceived by the intellect alone; they are never known by the senses <note>original: "promptis," referring to things ready at hand or accessible to the physical senses</note>; which is the one thing, I say, that would lead you above the mortal lords. 

While others, both among men and through the gifts of fortune, are suggested to be wealthy, famous, and even elevated to a changeable kingdom, they are carried to the judgment seat <term>tribunal: the raised platform where a judge or high official sat</term> by a public escort. Yet [true divinity] is rarely present: it is separated in certain inner chambers <note>original: "penetralibus," the most private or sacred parts of a temple or home</note> of its own Dignity, with witnesses removed from its Conception. Many and varied are those of high rank, yet they are more rarely seen in familiar imitation. 

What then shall I do (as an orator while the bow [is aimed] at others after those heavenly things which are mine: if I first consider your human opinion <note>original: "sententiam"</note>)? If two men are expelled by the Lord from such things as these, and little by little; and these things then seemed likely to be touched, lest in this way the house of anyone were denied to your Lord. Let no one be a stranger to another. Just as a shepherd looks after his sheep, or a horseman his horses, or a herdsman his oxen <note>original: "buffofua," likely a corruption of *bubus*</note>; whether they are of the wild beasts, or of the noble <note>original: "Gimmoru," possibly *gnarorum*</note>, or the common <note>original: "musuriu," likely *minuarium*</note>, so that they may be exchanged: they are measured in the thickets; he dwells among the sick, and thrives among the fit.

<margin>
<insert>the assembly</insert> <note>original Italian: "l'adunanza," a later marginal note likely referring to a gathering or congregation</note>
</margin>

Therefore, when shall I send forth my prayer? To whom, finally, shall I call out? Behold, do I offer a victim? And O Lord, the misery of the suppliants <term>supplicitorum: those who humbly beg or prostrate themselves before the divine</term>, who by favor of the good, instead of the evils of the adversaries, [pray] with the divine... When the Lord (as it is most piously written) forced the judgment <note>original: "arbitrium"</note> of the witness to be inscrutable? So that they might be anointed: through this head I enter, where he sat before; for I was like a Trojan in those things, frequently contemplating these inscrutable tortures. And perhaps, O Lord, to admit the grateful to the resting place. But truly, O Lord, who would believe that the captures are of the highest race, once known? He spoke for the sake of the faithful God: He spoke himself, having been taken from the miseries of the most persistent, and that man too. Indeed, this alone should be marveled at: that he might enjoy the fruit. More divine things in God: and as if through a thousand books for me. To the sacred oath of peace <note>original: "pacis sacramentum"</note>, O Lord, I pray...

...are strengthened from the head. They shimmer in ethereal ranks, though they are slower to the touch. Indeed, by their nature, their course is more sublime. <meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of divinity and the intermediary beings known as demons. While the previous page described the physical, airy composition of demonic bodies, this page shifts to a psychological and ontological comparison. It contrasts the "eternal equanimity" of the supreme Gods—who are immune to emotion and change—with the "passive" nature of demons, who share the emotional turbulence of human beings despite their immortality.</meta>

One imagines God to prosper and exult, and then conversely to be opposed and afflicted; likewise, that He is angry and indignant, or settled and joyful. For why would I make the human soul suffer similar movements of the heart and anxieties <note>original: "salomonis," likely a scribal error or corruption for "sollicitudinis" (anxiety)</note>, fluctuating in every tide of thought; its every turbulence and storm exulting shortly after in a tamed, clear tranquility? 

He [God], however, moving from the light, remains in nearly the same state of mind, possessing eternal equanimity <note>term: "equabilitate" (equanimity) — the state of being psychologically stable and unruffled, which Apuleius argues is a requirement for a perfect, unchanging deity</note>. He is driven by nothing, neither toward the experience of pain nor toward the limits of pleasure. Nor is He moved from His own proper state to any sudden condition; nor by any other force. For motion is hazardous for God; indeed, it is highly suspect. For motion belongs to things that are present; but that which could be seen to have been before perishes, and it appears to migrate from a prior state to another state. And since no one is capable of something new unless the prior things have perished, no change of a subject can occur without a prior diminution. 

Wherefore, many characteristics of either labor or love may be granted a temporal perfection. And yet, there is no indignation, nor any <unclear>distress</unclear>; He is distracted by no anguish, and experiences no excessive excitement. Instead, He is free from all passions of the soul, neither stung by pain nor rejoicing in anything; nor does He suddenly "will" or "not will" in any other way. 

And if this is justice, what then is divine? They define the middle-nature of demons. For they are said to be between us and the Gods in their location <unclear>as if in a position of height</unclear>, as intermediary demons. For they are held to possess immortality along with <unclear>fierce</unclear> passions. For just as with us, all things can serve as means to appease or irritate them; they are moved by their nature to be swayed, to be tamed, to be tumultuous, and <unclear>to be provoked</unclear>, according to the nature of the passions that arise. They are influenced by honors, and in all other things they vary in a manner similar to us. 

Indeed, as a genus they are:
**Animals by kind, rational by mind, subject to passions by soul, aerial by body, eternal by time.** <note>This is the famous "five-point definition" of demons provided by Apuleius, which became a standard reference in medieval and Renaissance demonology.</note>

From these characteristics, because they occupy a middle <unclear>ground</unclear> in the beginning...

<meta>This page continues Apuleius’s philosophical argument regarding the nature of demons. Having previously established that gods are unchanging and humans are mortal, he now focuses on demons as the middle ground: they possess the immortality of the gods but the emotional vulnerability (passions) of humans. This explains why they are the focus of various, often turbulent, religious rituals across different cultures.</meta>

They share the same nature with us. Finally, they are situated between the gods and mortal men; they differ from the former by their specific capacity for emotion <note>original: "passione." In this context, it refers to "passibility"—the ability to be affected by external things or to feel emotion, which the supreme gods lack.</note>. For this reason, they are not absurdly characterized, I believe, as "passible": because they are subject to the same disturbances of the mind as we are. From this also, faith must be granted to religion through various observations and the supplications of sacred rites. 

And there are some who enjoy this divine gift in nocturnal sacred rites—whether open or in hidden places—with sacrifices, ceremonies, or rituals. For instance, there are the Egyptian deities who are honored by those who wail for hunger <note>This likely refers to the cult of Isis and the ritual mourning for Osiris.</note>; the Greek deities with choruses of lamentation; and the Barbarian <note>In the classical sense, "Barbarian" refers to non-Greek/non-Latin speaking cultures, such as the Phrygians.</note> deities with the noise of cymbal-players and drummers and songs lasting three days throughout the regions. There are other differences in the sacred rites: the long, bound lines of processions, the silences of the ministrations, the duties of the priests, and the observations of the sacrifices. 

Now, the religions of the temples are filled with duties and opinions, with the rules and colors of the victims. Since all these things are solemn and rare throughout every recorded place, the deities are often deemed worthy of being recognized through dreams, prophecies, and certain oracles, just as they might neglect those who are prideful or disregard the sacred rites or dreams. Examples of this kind are available to me in abundance. 

These things are so celebrated and frequently discussed that no one attempts to describe them more commonly. In many cases, one would leave out more than would remain. There, then, where the path is suspect <unclear>...</unclear> where all speech is occupied. If certain faith and the knowledge of authors does not possess anything among all people, it would be better here to define them in Latin as "spirits" <note>original: "vanas spiritus"</note>, which they more closely call "demons" <note>term: "demones" (demons) — here used in the neutral classical sense of "daimon," a guiding spirit or intermediary power, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>, because they are constantly and fully concerned with the foretelling of fortunes, which they recognize from the immortal divinity. 

For the same term signifies that the human soul, even now while in the body, is called its own "demon." We say that this is what [Nature] adds to mortals. Therefore, a good desire of the soul is a "good demon" <note>original: "bonus demon"</note>. Whence some believe—as has already been said—that the blessed are called *eudaemonas* <note>original: "eudemonas" — from the Greek 'eu' (good) and 'daimon' (spirit).</note>: because a "good demon" is nothing other than the perfect virtue of the soul.

<summary>Apuleius argues that demons are emotionally "passible" intermediaries between gods and humans, explaining the variety of religious rituals used to appease them. He concludes by defining the "demon" as the indwelling spirit of human virtue, linking happiness (eudaemonia) to the soul's internal state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Apuleius’s exploration of the nature of "daemons" (spirits), moving from the general definition of their nature to a specific classification of how the human soul is categorized after death and the role of the personal guardian spirit.</meta>

There is another sense in which the term is used in our language, and I am not sure if it is interpreted well: from the danger within it, is a spirit called a **Genius** <note>original: "genium." In Roman belief, the Genius was the individual instance of the divine nature present in every person, place, or thing.</note>? This is what is said to be a person’s own soul, whose spirit is immortal; yet in a certain way, it is born with the human being, so that these very prayers with which we are born, and those who grasp the knees in supplication <note>original: "genua precantur." Grasping the knees was a traditional gesture of deep request or prayer in antiquity.</note>, seem to be joining body and soul, encompassing both within two words which are linked in a union.

There is also another kind of spirit, which is the human soul when it has left the body. In the ancient Latin language, they used to call these **Lemures**. From these Lemures, those who look after their descendants with a peaceful and quiet presence are possessed of the name **Lar** <term>Lar: (plural Lares) a protective household deity</term>, or the "familiar Lar." However, those who—because of no good merits in life—are punished by a sort of eternal wandering as a penalty for death, acting as a source of terror to good men and a plague to the wicked, most people call this kind **Larvae** <term>Larvae: malevolent, restless ghosts</term>. 

When it is uncertain what lot has fallen to a soul—whether it has become a *Lar* or a *Larva*—it is called by the name of the god **Manes** <term>Manes: the collective spirits of the dead, often called "the good ones" as a euphemism to avoid angering them</term>. The title of "god" is added here as an honor to the spirit. Indeed, they are only called gods if they have governed the course of life through a just and prudent path. Later, such spirits might be worshipped by humans with shrines and offerings, appearing to various people under different names: such as **Amphiaraus** in Boeotia, **Mopsus** in Africa, **Osiris** in Egypt, and others elsewhere as a **Genius**, or **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine and healing</note> everywhere. 

For the distribution of these common spirits—who once lived in a human body—was varied. But there is another type of spirit, far superior in dignity and of a higher rank, which is always free from the bonds and yokes of the body and is concerned with more excellent deeds. Among their number are **Sleep** and **Love**, who possess different powers in each person; some for waking, some for dreaming, others for deep slumber. 

From this higher abundance of spirits, **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher</note> asserts that individual guardians and watchers are assigned to every person for the conduct of their lives. These spirits assist us unseen, always present as witnesses to all our actions, judges of our deeds, and cooperators in a blessed life.

Therefore, it is no wonder if an excellent guardian was provided to Socrates, since he recognized and honored this guardian—his own master—not merely through the wisdom of speech. This private guardian, almost divine, expert, and familiar, argued against what should be avoided: he guarded against what was to be guarded, and forewarned of what was to be forewarned. Is it more noble? No wisdom, no long lineage, and no enviable wealth [makes it so]. For all these things, as I say, are **external** to us. <note>original: "aliæna" — meaning things that do not belong to the essence of the person, often translated as "foreign" or "alien."</note>

But all glory comes from one’s own merits, if it is of such a kind that one is not ashamed to display it. Therefore, consider all similar things as foreign to your account. Is he noble? Let him seek praise. Is he rich? I do not trust in fortune; that is more a matter of chance. Is he strong? He will be worn down by illness. Is he swift? He will perish in old age, and he will be no more.

But is he excellent in the goods of the mind? It is clear that to be this same person is to be both wise and well-advised. This same [wisdom] a person praises as his own. For this is not a heritage from a father, nor dependent on chance, nor stained by a popular vote, <note>original: "suffragio" — the author emphasizes that true merit is not granted by public opinion or elections.</note> nor failing with the body, nor changeable with age. 

Therefore, you who hear [this], from the beginning to the end, [is there anything] more brilliant than the genius of the wise? May you hear nothing foreign to your own praises. Just as those are accustomed [to do with] nobility, which they praise so that they are praised for the deeds of others <unclear>r</unclear> by their own record <unclear>r</unclear> which <unclear>r</unclear> they write as their own.

In olden times, the fatherland produced few things. Was it not rather the **son of Laertes** <term>Laertiadem: Odysseus (Ulysses), the hero of Homer's Odyssey, frequently used in philosophy as a symbol of the soul's journey toward wisdom.</term> who, acting as the author of fate for the Trojan <note>original: "dardanis" — referring to the Dardanians or Trojans.</note> wings, [found] a harbor for the Greek fleets? I speak of the son of Laertes: he protects his fatherland most recently. You have heard of the destruction [of Troy] and his praise. From that, he claims nothing for himself, neither through gentleness nor friendship nor most greedily. This whole [reputation], as it is said, is the proper possession of this praise. 

Nor does anything else teach a man in the same way as he who always wished [to turn] from the banquet to **prudence**, <note>original: "prudentiā" — practical wisdom or foresight.</note> through which, having laid aside [pleasures], he interprets the way of life. Therefore, these same things accompany him: they undergo all horrors; they overcome all adversities. Indeed, with Wisdom as his helper, the state of pleasure is ground down and cast aside. It is said of the good alone: if tossed to the elements, they fight and ascend. 

With this same wisdom as a companion, he sailed past **Scylla** <note>A multi-headed sea monster from the Odyssey.</note> and was not taken. He rose again from **Charybdis** <note>OCR: "Cāberi" — a whirlpool monster; the text suggests he survived the "resurrection" from its depths.</note> and was not held back. He drank the cup of **Circe** <note>The sorceress who turned men into swine; Odysseus resisted her magic with the help of a holy herb.</note> and was not transformed. He approached the **Lotus-eaters** <note>original: "locofagos" — people who ate a fruit that caused forgetfulness and apathy.</note> and did not remain. He heard the **Sirens** and did not go to them.

# The Book of the Philosopher Hermes Trismegistus
## Begins;

Asclepius. This Asclepius is like the sun to me <unclear>as</unclear>. God has brought you to us, O Asclepius, so that you might take part in this divine discourse. Truly, it is right that he did so, for we have made every effort, by the divine power, to appear with the purification and religious piety required for divine matters. If only you could see Tat <note>original: "tathane" — a scribal variation of Tat, the son and student of Hermes.</note>, in whose mind the whole light of all goodness shines. Many of those who come are good, yet they are not one and the same as the All. For one thing follows from another by the consent of their Master: so that the Master is one, and is one and all. For both are so in harmony with each other that one cannot be separated from the other. But in the coming discourse, you will learn this most diligently. Now, O Asclepius, step forward a little and call whoever is missing to us.

When Hammon <note>original: "amona" — King Hammon, another regular student of Hermes.</note> and Tat <note>original: "sytrophio" — likely a corruption of "Tat" or a reference to a companion.</note> had entered, Hermes the Egyptian <note>original: "Ermes gipteus" — Hermes Trismegistus was legendary as an Egyptian sage.</note> said: "Let no spirit <note>original: "dmonu" — referring to lesser spirits or distractions that might interrupt a sacred rite.</note> hinder you. While we have many written records for the ages, just as we have many writings on <term>nature</term> <note>original: "physica" — the study of the natural world.</note> and spiritual matters for our most beloved and dear son, the urge now moves us to write what is good. Especially since no stranger has been called besides Hammon. For the religious discourse on so great a matter should not be violated by the intrusion of many people. For it is a mind filled with the majesty of the divine spirit, and it is a confusion to publish it to the masses."

When Hammon had also entered the room, and they were filled with the religion of the gods and divine matters, they stood with venerable and full presence of mind. A divine desire hung over their souls. O Asclepius, how great is the immortal soul! It is not of a single form or appearance like other things. Or rather, it is its very self.

"Do you not say, Trismegistus, that the soul is of a single form?"
"O Asclepius, how quickly you have slipped from the true reasoning I just gave. I do not say this: that all things are one and one is all things, insofar as all things were in the Creator before he created all things. Therefore, he is one and all things, or rather, he is the Creator of all. In this whole dispute, take care to remember what has been said of the heavens, the earth, the water, and the air. For that which is perceived by the senses is made life-giving, which is said of the self and of the seed."

<meta>This page continues the opening discourse of the Asclepius. Hermes is explaining the cosmological structure of the universe, specifically the relationship between the celestial "nourisher" and the terrestrial "receiver," and how God governs the world through spirit and soul. It follows the introductory gathering of disciples mentioned on the previous page.</meta>

Indeed, if anything descends from on high, it is a **generator**; that which remains above is a **nourisher**. Earth alone, consisting in itself, is the **receiver** of all things and the restorer of all kinds of things that she receives. 

Therefore, this whole (as we recall) which is "all things," or whose boundaries are the world's, is contained and encompassed by nature. Thus, the lover of wisdom is full of every image of intelligible things. We see that a great deal of the invisible species clings to us, uniting with us, so that the whole of the world seems to exist for its own good. 

It appears that the whole of the world is formed; its **four elements** <note>original: "elementa sua quat(ur)" — the classic elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> reach to its very edges. For this one world, there is **one soul** <term>Anima Mundi</term> <note>The "Soul of the World," a vital force that permeates all nature.</note>, through one God. Nor can so many species added to the mind prevail as when the <insert>sacred</insert> cup is breathing <note>original: "calice spirante" — likely a reference to the 'Crater' or mixing bowl of the soul mentioned in Hermetic lore.</note>; for the divine perception of divine things by the senses is uncertain. It is most like someone trying to hold onto something while in a rushing, headlong river. 

By this, it happens that the mind's grasp fails not only the listeners, but the very appearance of external authorities might perish for the sake of the treatise itself. Behold, concerning sensible and <term>indemonstrable</term> <note>Truths that cannot be proven by logic alone but must be experienced or revealed.</note> things, the world divides its own increase among all bodies, which the sun and moon serve. 

Others, however, are spirits in everything that exists in the world; God himself is the governor and the effector. And as was said to all, God is called the "governor" because he guides all the works of his hand. Through the world and from the soul of kinds, all space is filled by the nature of things. 

The world was prepared by God so that it might offer every kind of form. For by imagining the world through these species, they lead the world through the generation of elements toward another state, preferred by God above all visible things. Moreover, divine things hanging from above are divided into spirit. This is said because the whole world preserves its own **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus" — here referring to a literal animating breath or essence.</note> so that it may be one solidified mass of a kind, with all things moving forward through spirit. 

For they know God, who makes himself manifest through spirit for the purification of the kind, and they know that he willed things to be similar to humans and to all things that generate themselves through spirits similar to their own world-kind. It is also known that there is another, better thing: the servant of likeness. They take care regarding the names of the spirits, from which one rejoices in benefit and is diminished by adversity and divinity every day...

<meta>This page continues the discourse in the Asclepius where Hermes Trismegistus explains the hierarchy of the universe. Following the discussion of the "Soul of the World" and the divine "Crater" (mixing bowl), Hermes now describes how divine nature preserves the universe through "genera" (kinds) and "species" (forms), and how humans occupy a unique, miraculous position between the divine and the material.</meta>

...in its true root, that which specifically preserves the safety of the universe is **species** <term>species</term> <note>In this context, "species" refers to the "ideal forms" or "types" that give individual things their shape and character.</note> through all the species of its own nature. The heaven itself is full of God.

The aforementioned **kinds** <note>original: "gena," likely a contraction of "genera" — the broad categories of being.</note> are assigned even to the regions of the spheres; for they are immortal lives, they are spirits. **Spirit**, however, is a part of a kind in which, insofar as it is not fixed but a flowing kind, it is seen to be produced of itself. 

Just as various kinds are immortal, not all species are immortal. For Divinity begets both **Reason** <term>Ratio</term> and the immortal species. Indeed, while eternity belongs to the kinds, some are preserved through the species: [Nature] preserves the cycle of their birth. Therefore, species are mortal, just as man is mortal, yet he is also immortal in part.

Out of these, in all things, every kind of spirit is mixed; they are that certain thing which is mixed. Likewise, those things made from them reach an end. This, therefore, which was the **Soul of the World** <note>original: "animā dūi," likely "anima mundi."</note>, is shared by demons and by men, and by all similar things in their own species. For it is impossible for bodies to be shaped without divine power. The species of perfections cannot prevail without the help of **demons** <note>original: "demonū" — here meaning "daemons," intermediary spirits or guardians, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>; they themselves cannot be like the condition of heaven. Having distributed the ranks of demons, by whose discipline they carry the form in their species: they entrust another divine kind of species and associate them as they have similar conditions.

Those demons whose species belong to the kind over which they preside are called the **rational kind** of demons.

It must be known that all things from the air are multiform and varied according to species, which the spirit itself—sprinkled from above by the aforementioned name—animates with a vital spirit. It also makes many things through nature. For this reason, it is established by God.

Because Nature, which is of divine origin <note>original: "dūis mortis" — possibly "divine death," suggesting the soul's descent into the mortal realm.</note>, is joined to the gods by divine religion and to the demons who serve in these turns. But humans who hate the purity of their own kind are also the remaining spirits of men. They will be like these according as they join themselves to the kinds of spirits.

Therefore, O **Asclepius**, **man is a great miracle** <note>original: "magnū miraculū est [homo]" — one of the most famous lines in Hermetic philosophy, celebrating human potential.</note>, a living being to be adored and honored. For he passes into the nature of God as if he were himself a spirit, just as the gods. This [kind] of demons...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue known as the *Asclepius*, part of the Hermetic tradition. Having previously discussed the Soul of the World and the role of demons, Hermes Trismegistus now focuses on the unique, "miraculous" nature of humanity, which stands as a bridge between the divine and the material worlds.</meta>
