What does he know of himself, once he recognizes that he has sprung from the same source? In what part of himself does this lie? He may despise himself in part, yet he is established with the value of **divinity** <term>divinitas</term>. O human! How much more happily tempered is your nature, joined from two natures! <note>Hermes is referring to the "double nature" of humanity: part mortal/material and part immortal/divine.</note> Man is joined [to the gods] by that part of himself in which he excels; he is one with them. He despises [the worldly part of himself], since he knows he was born for all things by a celestial **disposition** <term>dispositio</term> <note>original: "dispositio'm" — the divine ordering or arrangement of the universe.</note>; he binds himself in love to his own kind. He sighs for the other part of his being.

And how much more happily is he placed in a middle position! So that he may love what is below him, and he himself may be loved by those superior to him. He cultivates them in turn; he is bound by a pleasure of nourishment, and by joined merits and confident hands he is looked down upon by none. All things are permitted to him. Nor does he see the highest things as being far away; it is as if he is mixed with the keenness of the **demons** <note>In this context, *daemones* are helpful intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> through his own sagacity. With his intention, since no fog of the air obscures it, nor does the density of the earth hinder his work, nor does the profound depth of the sea dull his sight, he is the same everywhere and is everywhere present. He distributes to all the kinds and their living beings that emerge from the root; they possess **reason** <term>ratio</term>. Among living beings, however, from one kind there is one root. They are similar. But certain ones are from double natures, others from single ones.

The nourishment by which they are sustained is two-fold: of the **soul** <term>anima</term> and of the body, of which living beings consist. By this the machine of the world is always changed by movement. Your bodies, too, are driven by the **spirit** <term>spiritus</term> of the world and are increased by its nourishment. With the spirit, by which all things are full: it is ready for all things, and it gives life to all, with sense added to human intelligence. This fourth part was granted to man alone from the ether. And concerning the living beings now: only five senses reach toward the understanding of divine reason; it increases and lifts them up. And since I will speak regarding the common sense a little later and explain our view to you—for it is most holy and great, and **Mind** <term>Nous</term> <note>original: "noy" (Greek: νοῦς) — the highest form of intellect or divine perception.</note> is no less than that which is by divinity—if there is space for you, I will open it. For divinity in itself is a rare mystery concerning the state and origin of all things, which he deigned to grant to humans alone; he granted the divine spirit to man as a son to his own spirit.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue known as the *Asclepius*. Hermes Trismegistus has been explaining that man possesses a unique, dual nature that allows him to perceive both the material world and the divine realm. Here, he distinguishes between true intelligence and mere reasoning, and begins to explain why God created humanity to dwell within the material world.</meta>

...so that, in that state, divine intelligence might perceive through the senses, just as it does through divine sense. Is this reserved for the **gods alone**? What a great intelligence this is! For sense is not uniform for every human being who is bound to a body. Not all people, O Asclepius, have attained true **intelligence**.

But an **imaginary reasoning** <note>original: "imaginaria ratiocinatio" — a false or superficial way of thinking that lacks true spiritual insight</note> that is impure thinks of nothing with true reason. It deceives, giving birth to malice in the mind, and transforms the best of animals into the nature of wild beasts. Now, concerning sense and intelligence, and even concerning the spirit, I shall provide the whole explanation to you.

For of all animals, man alone is **twofold**. One part of him is simple, which the Greeks call **essential** <term>ousiōdēs</term> <note>original: OYCIWΔHC — pertaining to the true essence or substance of a thing</note>, and which we call the form of divine likeness. But the other part is **complex**, which the Greeks call **material** <term>hylikon</term> <note>original: YΛIKON — relating to matter or the physical world</note>, and we call worldly. From this material part, the body was made, which surrounds and governs that which we have called the divine element in man—namely, **reason** <note>original: "rōy" / "rationem"</note>. In this divine part, the whole mind of divinity consists, standing alone with its own kin—that is, with pure minds—though it is hemmed in by a loathing for the body.

"Why then, O Trismegistus, was it necessary for man to be established in the world, and not in that part where God is, especially since you said the highest happiness is found there?"

You ask rightly, O Asclepius! And we pray to the Lord to grant us the ability to provide an explanation. For since all things depend upon His will—especially those great matters that deal with the highest peak of reality—they are brought together through the desperation of reason. <note>This suggests that human logic alone cannot reach these truths without divine help.</note>

Listen then, Asclepius. The Lord and Shaper of all—whom we call God—when He had made the **second god** <note>In Hermetic thought, the "second god" is often the Cosmos or the Sun, a visible manifestation of the invisible Creator.</note> from Himself, who could be seen and felt (I call him the **sensible** god, not because he himself feels—for we will discuss whether he feels or not at another time—but because he can be seen), since He brought forth this creation from Himself as the first and this second one, and it appeared beautiful and most full of all goodness, He loved it as a part of His own divinity. Therefore, because He is so great and good, He willed that there be another who could contemplate the one He had made from Himself. At the same time, by His will, He created man as an imitation of His own reason and diligence. For he...

<meta>This page continues the discourse between Hermes Trismegistus and his disciple Asclepius. Having established that man is a dual being of soul and body, Hermes now explains why this arrangement exists: so that humanity can serve as a bridge, caring for the earth while worshiping the divine.</meta>

And this is the highest perfection, as if to have willed and to have perfected everything in a single stroke: a pious and prompt **wisdom** <term>sophia</term> <note>original: "sophia" — the Greek word for wisdom, often personified in mystical texts</note>. And so, when I began to hand this down—since no one can look upon all things with the diligence required in this worldly realm, for such vision has altogether perished—no one living in this **bodily house** <note>original: "corporea domo" — a metaphor for the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul</note> is able to remain looking upon what is truly good and right; he ought instead to pity those who are [merely] healthy in body.

Therefore, man was reformed in regard to the body as well. That is, he was made from a **soul** <term>anima</term> and a **mortal nature** <note>original: "ex anima et mortali natura"</note>, so that by this reformed path he might perceive both of his origins: he might be able to wonder at and pray to celestial things, and to cultivate and govern earthly things. For now, I speak of mortal things—not merely water and earth, which are two of the four elements subject to us. For man has his own [purpose]... and here was the shepherd and the building of our religion.

It is possible for those navigating by the community and convenience of the elements... which is however firm it may be in the **union** <unclear>nuptio</unclear> and protection of the world, namely water and earth. Because in its part, it preserved the discipline, knowledge, and use of the whole world. But God did not wish the world itself to be imperfect; for our [understanding] of God is received in full. By His will, He made it common. Nor is it credible that what pleased God could be displeasing to Him, since it was a **seed** <note>original: "simẽ" for "semen" — referring to the divine spark or creative principle</note>, that is, the fullest seed, preserved for many years. These people, led by outward appearances so that they reject others through fear, stop to hear how man may be nourished, or how through so many ages he might be held in light or worship. By hearing and by work...

<margin>1 Love</margin>
Beloved Asclepius? There is but one worship of the gods, since He Himself is in the One. There is one frequenting of services. No other earthly animal perceives the divine <unclear>hearings</unclear> except for man alone. For by the admirations, adorations, praises, and services of men, the celestial beings are nourished and delighted. Nor is it feared that the **choirs of the Muses** <term>musarum choris</term> <note>the Nine Muses of Greek myth, representing the arts and sciences, here seen as divine gifts to help man praise God</note> were sent from the highest divinity into man's narrow frame. 

But how would the worldly courts be seen if He had neglected the sweetness of melodies? Rather, it was so that man might be celebrated with musical praises—he who alone looks upon God as the source of all things. And so, through our accepted praises, he might serve the sweetness of the highest parts of the earth. That very thing which we think to be the smallest part will be perfect through such an expectation of wonders.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the Latin translation of the *Asclepius*, a core text of the Hermetic tradition. ...care. However, whoever is infused with the nature of a dual **blending** <note>original: "refusionis" — a technical term in this context referring to the pouring together or merging of divine spirit and material substance</note> and intelligence into the mass of the body, does so for the purpose of caring for these inferior elements set before him. They say that Man—not because he is common or because he is mortal in part—but if he is made an operative composite, he might rightly admire the whole world through this composite action. For he alone could not have received both natures in himself without some middle ground. He is formed through both so that he may behold both the presence of the divine and the steps of **divinity** <term>divinitas</term>. By reason, truly, it is argued from here that he may ascend not only through heavenly **subtlety** <note>original: "tenuitate" — refers to the "thinness" or ethereal quality of spiritual substance compared to heavy matter</note>, but also desires to unite himself with divinity through his persistence. For there is an incredible persistence in this matter; especially for such great things to be grasped by holier minds. The superior man. That is, by his own certain and proper diligence, he ensures that both he and the world are an ornament to one another; so that from this order the divine dispensation of the world, which is more truly called **KOSMOS** <term>kosmos</term> <note>original: "KOSMOS" — the Greek word for "order" or "beauty," used here to describe the universe as a harmonious system</note>, might be seen. Such a man knows himself: he knows also the world. That is to say, let him remember what belongs to his divine parts, what things he must use, and what things he must rather restrain. Let him recognize these things, giving the greatest praise and thanks to God, whose image he venerates, not being ignorant that he himself is also the second **image of God** <note>In Hermetic philosophy, God is the first entity, the World is the second, and Man is the third, each reflecting the one above</note>. For God has two images: the world and Man. From this it follows that since he is a single **framework** <note>original: "compago" — a structure or joining together of parts</note>: partly in that he is divine—consisting of soul, sense, spirit, and reason—he appears to be made of the higher elements. Thus, he is at last able to look toward heaven. But in the worldly part which remains—consisting of fire, water, and earth—he remains mortal in his earthly care, seeing all his worldly things and the divine service. For thus his magnitude is divine in one part, while on the other hand, he is made mortal, consisting in a body. Moreover, the measure of both of these—that is, of man—is before all...

<meta>This page continues the discourse of Hermes Trismegistus in the *Asclepius*. Having established man as a "middle being," the text now explores the specific duties of this dual nature: the service to the material world and the worship of the divine.</meta>

**Religion** <note>original: "religio" — in this context, it refers to the bond of piety and duty between the human and the divine</note>, since it is of perfect goodness. By the same reasoning, it then seems to be professed.
If against the **greed** <term>cupiditas</term> of others, since in this matter there is an unequal vice.
For its gifts are alien to all the divine parts of kinship; everything that is possessed by whatever corporal greed.
These are not rightly called "possessions" <note>original: "possessione" — meaning things truly owned as part of one's essence</note> because they were not born with us. If they began to be possessed by us later,
therefore they are not called our possessions. Because what was outside of us was alien to man; even the body, as we also seek after it.
and we manage that which is closer to our desire.
Truly, while man holds the mind as the leader of **reason** <term>ratio</term>, he has thus far been obliged to be the beholder of **divinity** <term>divinitas</term> in that part of him which is joined to the mortal, [acting as] the messenger of the **lower world** <term>mundus inferior</term> for the purpose of preserving, managing, and cultivating it.
For so that man might be most perfect in both parts: although he consists of and is formed from the elements of both parts—with two hands and feet and other members of the body—he serves the lower creation <note>original: "feti" — likely a contraction for "foetui" (offspring/creation) or "effectui" (effect)</note>, that is, the earthly world.
But by those parts through which the sense of the mind intends and provides, by whose reason he knows and looks up to divine things.
From which it happens that he is made stronger in the investigative inquiry into such diverse effects of qualities and quantities. (Truly he is slowed by the heavy and excessive burden of the body.)
These then are the causes why [these things] cannot be well-perceived through providence. By this duty he is reformed, so that through such service and obedience—which is the purpose set by the highest God—they may adore the world by preserving the world and piously worshiping God.
Worthy and competent, he serves the will of God in both; he is to be adorned by such a gift in proper order. If indeed these are the works of order: he who with diligence forms and increases the world toward beauty, joins the will of all his works with the form which He <note>Referring to the Creator/God</note>...

<summary>This passage describes humanity's dual obligation to maintain the beauty of the physical Earth while remaining spiritually devoted to the divine. It argues that material wealth is "alien" to our true nature, whereas our true purpose is found in managing the world as God's representatives.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse from the *Asclepius*, where Hermes Trismegistus explains the human condition. <margin>By this aid</margin>
Formed by the **Divine Mind**, man responded to the miracle of his own body with divine labor and help—unless he should fear not to be changed by that very means. For how could we, who hope to be changed if it pleases the divine, [do so] except by the purest of goods? This means that being stripped and purified from the custody of the world, and absolved of mortal merits, we may be stationed in the higher part—that is, the divine seats—as pure and familiar beings. This is permitted to those who become like gods, O Trismegistus; for this is the reward for those living diligently under God and in harmony with the world.

However, for the spirit that avoids this path, even if it has seen divine things and others, it shall undergo a foul and unworthy migration into other bodies. As is lamented at the first step, O Trismegistus, the hope of future eternity is put at risk by an impure life. 

But to some, this seems incredible; to others, a fable; and to others, perhaps, it is even a matter of ridicule. For death is sweet in this bodily life if one has been greedy for possessions. Therefore, death holds a man back "with a twisted neck" <note>original: "obtorto collo" — a Latin idiom meaning to be dragged along by force or against one's will, suggesting the soul's reluctance to leave the material world</note>, as they say. He moves through that part of himself which is mortal, and the immortal malice of the world does not recognize him without some part of divinity. 

Therefore, when he stands apart as if predominating, he is not diluted by any of these habits through the study of simple **philosophy** <term>philosophia</term>. This study alone consists of frequent contemplation in order to know divinity through holy **religion** <term>religio</term>. 

For many people confuse these things in many ways. Because many make philosophy unworkable, or they confuse it with various reasons, O Asclepius. Clever men recommend it through various disciplines that are difficult to grasp: through **arithmetic** <term>arithmetika</term> <note>original: "ARITHMETIKHN" — the Greek science of numbers</note>, music, and geometry. But one should study pure **philosophy** as that which depends only upon divine religion. 

As for the other sciences, it is enough to wonder at how the **restoration** <term>apocatastasis</term> <note>original: "apocatastasis" — the cyclic return or restoration of the stars to their original positions</note> of the stars, their predetermined stations, and the cycles of their movements are fixed by numbers; and to wonder at the dimensions, qualities, and quantities of the earth and the sea...

<summary>Hermes explains that a pure life leads the soul to a divine state, while an impure life leads to reincarnation in "foul" bodies. true philosophy is defined as the simple study of God through religion, rather than the complex distractions of mathematics or music.</summary>

In the time of being born and procreating, which they possess for a long time, the act is an everlasting nature. There was also an equality of nature which had even conceived before.

<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of the Asclepius, a foundational text of Hermeticism. The previous page concluded a discussion on the "Divine Mind" and the necessity of approaching the divine with a "simple mind" rather than the complex fallacies of the sophists. This page shifts to the nature of the "Place" (space) of the world and addresses the classic theological problem of why evil (malice) exists if God is the creator.</meta>

<margin>For</margin>
it possesses in itself the one and the one <note>The original Latin *vnum atq[ue] vnam* implies both the masculine and feminine aspects of unity, a common Hermetic concept where the divine source is androgynous or all-encompassing</note>. This, therefore, to be without another, belongs only to the one capable of generating <note>original: *generabile*</note>. But truly, those things which have only the capacity for conceiving one thing toward the union of another nature are to be so distinguished. Thus, this place of the world, with those things which are in it, may appear not to be one, because it has in itself every nature of the whole.

Moreover, I speak of a "place" in which all things are. For none of these things could have existed if a place were lacking that could support them all. Therefore, a place must be provided even for the things that have been. Neither quality, nor quantity, nor positions, nor diverse effects could have belonged to a thing that is nowhere.

Thus, even if the world is not one in itself, it nevertheless possesses all natures, so that through this it simultaneously provides form to the things spread out for the purpose of conceiving. This, then, is to prescribe the whole quality of nature. Then, if I should ask, it is not God [who is malice], and the quality of material nature is secondary. Likewise, <term>malignity: "malitia" in the original Latin, often translated as "evil" or "wickedness" in a philosophical sense</term> is the same in itself as anything secondary.

Therefore, do not say, O Asclepius, what is said by many—
<margin>O world!</margin>
that God, as the author and governor of all nature, cannot banish malice <note>original: *malitiam*</note>. To them, it must be answered: there is no fault at all in the Cause <note>The "Cause" refers to the First Cause or the Creator (God)</note>, and for this reason, they render an account. For they themselves say that God ought to have freed the world from malice. For it is so present in the world that it seems to be the world itself. Yet provision and caution were taken by the supreme God in a more rational way: at that time when He deigned to assist the minds of men with sense, discipline, and intelligence.

For in these things, by which we stand above the other animals, we alone are able to avoid malice, frauds, deceits, and vices. For before all these things, man is implicated in that which they live to assist. Man is fortified <note>original: *praemunitive*</note> by reason, divine intelligence, and prudence.

Whatever things appear within it arrange themselves through a diligent order <note>original: *ratio*</note> in their place, even from that depth which cannot be seen.

Properly speaking, although it seems to have a quality in many places, it is only through the forms of the spheres—in whose images things seem to be engraved—that the world is rendered visible, as if it were a painted image. Thus, truth itself is always invisible to itself. Wherever a part of it, or a pure place, is in the sphere of anyone, it is spoken of. That which comes through sight is said to come from the things at the bottom of the sphere. Otherwise, the lower things would then appear. Here, therefore, are the principal and more ancient things, appearing as if they were corporeal or...

<meta>This page continues the Hermetic dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and Asclepius. ...in contemplation: nor shall we name any of these things with a defined name. 

If indeed this is true, which is the act of His own <term>spirit <note>original: *spiritu*; in this context, the animating breath or life-force of the divine</note></term>: declaring the sound of these things, whether by will or by sense, which is perceived from without through the senses. But in a certain way, I have proposed the whole substance in these small syllables. A definition and a written record have been made so that they might reside in our memory. For I do not hope that by the dwelling of the whole, or by the assent of all that lives, or even the Lord, that the One can be called by many proposed names. By what name, then, or rather by every name, should He be called? Since indeed, if they are one and all things, it must be that either the name is "All," or that all things are His names, so that He Himself is called by the names of all things. 

He alone, therefore, as all things, is most full of the <term>fecundity <note>original: *fecunditate*; the capacity to produce offspring or new life</note></term> of both sexes. Pregnant by His own will, He is at once giving birth to a <term>fetus <note>original: *fetum*; here used metaphorically for the created world or "the offspring of His will"</note></term> of things; for His will is the surpassing <term>goodness <note>original: *bonitas*</note></term> of all.

And this goodness of all things is that very divinity, a <term>natured nature <note>original: *naturata natura*; a famous philosophical concept where God is seen as the nature that gives birth to all other natures</note></term>. So that all things are just as they were, and were, and shall be; nature defines from within itself the sufficiency of being born. This, therefore, O Asclepius, is His own <term>virtue <note>original: *virtus*; meaning His inherent power or excellence</note></term>, whereby and how all things are made everywhere.

Therefore, when you speak, O <term>Trismegistus <note>Thrice-Greatest; the title of the speaker, Hermes</note></term>: it concerns not only the Lord, Asclepius, but all things animate and inanimate. For it is impossible for any of them to be unfruitful. If <term>fecundity <margin>masculine power</margin></term> were taken away from all things that exist, it would be impossible for them to always be what they are. 

I say this of all things, for indeed I speak of sense, and I speak of the world itself, and all born things that are conserved as a gift. For procreation is full of both sexes. And to Him, at every time—or what is more truly "Goodness"—it is incomprehensible, whether it should be rightly called desire, or benevolence, or both. This, therefore, is truer than truth and more manifest than what I have already grasped by the mind.

<meta>This page continues the Hermetic dialogue from the previous page, shifting from the general "mixture" of nature to the specific composition of the human soul and the role of spiritual instruction in achieving immortality.</meta>

In certain matters: it is not that the desires of cravings and other faulty vices reside within the souls of men. —and because he is formed from a mortal nature, he is also subject to all mortality. He himself sees religion and a holy mind, provided that he regards and guards all things with a grateful affection.

If we divide these few things with a pious mind: nothing should be said concerning the vision of God, lest the speech of those contemplating it be violated by sacrilege. And since the divine discourse tells us of the knowledge and fellowship of men and God: recognize this, **O Asclepius**, concerning man: The Lord and Father (or that which is the highest) is the artisan of the gift of religion; thus Man was a gift, if he respects his own grace through the first path, and not only illuminates but also <unclear>washes</unclear>. Nor is he only confirmed toward Him through his own virtue. 

"Do you wonder, **O Asclepius**?" 

"Not at all," he said, "nor is it in difficulty as it is for many. And to pour it out, **O Trismegistus**, I who gladly assent to your words, I declare that man to be most happy who has attained such great happiness. Nor is he undeservedly worthy of a miracle, in whom is the greatest of all gifts: the Good, manifest in all its overflowing from the most pure..."

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Hermes Trismegistus and Asclepius. Having previously discussed the judgment of the soul and the nature of divine punishment, the text now transitions into a discourse on the relationship between the Sun, the divine essence, and the eternal governance of the world.</meta>

Therefore, at that time, the good and the bad among these are separated. Some seem to think that the aforementioned religion shines through the worship and veneration of God as if it were sent from heaven and hoped for by the confidence of their own belief; whereas all human piety is actually placed under the light of eternity. But the Sun itself is not merely of its own magnitude; it illuminates because **divinity** <note>original: *divinitas*</note> and goodness are diffused from it. 

But regard this god, O Asclepius, who governs the world, by whom worldly living beings are illuminated—whether they be eternal or subject to change—they are seen also in another world as that which always was, is, and shall be. Nothing in the world is mortal, for the divine always appears to be living; that is, he is as he is, and just as he is everlasting to the world, he is always living for the living being. Thus, there is no place for mortality. 

Therefore, it should be most clear to men that **eternity** <note>original: *aeternitatem*</note> must exist if it always lives with the world. Since the whole world is everlasting, let the Sun also live as its eternal governor, whether as the one who presides over or the **steward** <note>original: *dispensator*; an administrative role often used to describe how God manages the universe</note> of those things that live. God, because he is the everlasting governor of the world and of the living things in the world, lives as the steward of the living. At the same time, he dispenses **vitality** <note>original: *vitia*; likely a transcription error for *vitalia* or *vitalitatem*, given the context of life-giving</note> to living things.

Moreover, this is provided by the law of light in the way I shall say: For in the living world itself, he preserves the eternity of the world; because of this, that which is not corrupted remains stable. He grants the everlastingness of living to all and, as if he himself established the world, he is the steward of all things. Here, however, are those things that are below, and this is the place of all things governed under the Sun; and the world itself reminds us that it consists of a **double essence** <note>original: *duplici essentia*; referring to the dual nature of the universe, being both material/changeable and spiritual/eternal</note>. He himself is immutable from eternity despite corruptible things, giving life to all things that are within himself. 

Distributing to the world even in appearances and species, increased through the essence of the Sun and the descent of the stars, they rule all spaces. Likewise, these things are written by law; but it is necessary for eternity to overcome those things that are within: a **vigor** <note>original: *pigoris*; likely *vigoris*</note> that recognizes variety. Through celestial revolutions, they return to the same place; the spaces renew their return. And he [rules] the world itself with a quickening spirit or by the course of the experience of eternity. 

The end.

<meta>This page continues the discourse between Hermes and Asclepius regarding the nature of the cosmos. The previous page established the Sun as the eternal governor of the world and the steward of vitality; here, the text delves deeper into the philosophical mechanics of stability versus movement, and how eternity contains time.</meta>

<margin>
<note>original: magnitudinem per ipsum ponit</note>
He places magnitude through himself.
</margin>

...is preserved by the **regulator** <note>original: *ordinatore*; refers to the divine ordering principle of the universe</note>. Order and time are renewed for things because, as they are in the world, they are nourished. They create birth. For all things that already exist, nothing is stable, nothing is fixed, and nothing is immobile. There is no safety for those being born, nor for those departing, nor for those living; and deservedly so, for He alone exists in Himself and from Himself. He is not [moved], but is whole, full, and perfect. 

Therefore, because His stability is firm, He cannot be moved by the impulse of others nor by a change in place, seeing as He is God. And without Him, He is alone—unless someone should dare to say that He came into existence by His own motion, when rather it is **eternity** <note>original: *eternitas*</note> itself that is immobile, in which the **agitation** <note>original: *agitatio*; a technical term for the constant flux or restlessness of the material world</note> of all times is overcome, and through which the agitation of all times takes its beginning. 

From which source this stability came, while eternity remains ever similar, it is established that the **world** <note>original: *mundum*</note> is moved: do we not call it sensible? It has a mutable nature. The image of this God—what would this be? It is the world, unmoved within eternity. 

**Time** <note>original: *tempus*</note>, however, possesses the measure and number of its own stability. Because it is always in motion, it exists through that time and through the vicissitudes of living. Therefore, what are they? A stable, immobile, and fixed eternity, into which time—which is mobile—perpetually returns through its agitation. Through its mobility, **form** <note>original: *species*; referring to the visible appearance of things in the physical realm</note> is seen. It results that even eternity itself, though immobile, through the time in which form exists, seems to be equalized in its agitation. 

Thus it happens that the stability of eternity seems to be moved, and by the mobility of time, it is made stable by a fixed law of its course. So it is, while it is credible that time, being equalized, falls back into itself immovably. For by the stability of time in its magnitude, there is an "immobile agitation." For magnitude itself is the immobile law. This same thing is such that it is not subject to defined senses, but is **beyond the senses** <note>original: *persensibile*; literally "thoroughly sensible" but used here to mean beyond the grasp of ordinary human perception</note> and inestimable. It can neither be sustained, nor known, nor investigated. Where will it be to which...

<summary>This page explores the paradoxical relationship between eternity and time, arguing that while God and eternity are perfectly stable, they provide the framework and "fixed law" that allows the world and time to move.</summary>
<keywords>eternity, time, stability, motion, divine law, world, Asclepius, Hermes Trismegistus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue from the *Asclepius*, a Hermetic work. and from where, and who, and of what sort He is: this has been discussed. But He existed in the highest **stability** <note>original: *stabilitate*; in Hermetic thought, God is the unmoved mover, the point of absolute rest from which motion begins</note>: and He is stability itself: just as **eternity** <note>original: *aeternitas*</note> is of itself: just as unity and unity are one. Because all things which are sensible in the world can be seen. Eternity, which alone is perceived by sight <note>meaning the "eye of the mind"</note>, and the quality of the sensible sense would be given through the gods rarely, so that from the quality of the voice, the quality through its own sense is directed toward truth alone. Its truth in the world does not even attempt to obtain credit.

I give the greatest thanks to God, because I give the highest thanks concerning the divine nature, who has illuminated me, a seer, with his divinity. However, the **intellect** <term>intellectus: in Hermetic philosophy, this is the higher faculty of spiritual understanding or "nous," distinct from mere logical reasoning</term> of these things differs from **sense** <term>sensus: the perception of the physical world or the cosmic consciousness shared by all things</term> in that intellect is established for the purpose of loving and demonstrating the sense of the world. Yet they are mutually connected to each other. The intellect of the world reaches toward eternity and the gods who are to be known, who are above it. And if it happens to men (as it does to some through religion who see purely within)—since it is possible to return through sense if any way is open—the world itself, standing in its own prudence, is very narrow to us, though it seems filled with abundance to the most wise. 

For God cannot be seen or summoned in the visible world as if from a **machine** <note>original: *in machina*; a likely reference to the "deus ex machina" of ancient theater, where a god was lowered onto the stage by a crane. Hermes suggests God is not a mechanical actor in the physical world</note>; thus, under the name of **Venus**, something might appear to be less, or seem to have been able to exist or have existed. Because the members of the world are also very full, the world itself is full and perfected with bodies. Their forms are divided, and they have their own species by which they are great; of these, one is larger than another and another smaller, and they differ between the strong and the delicate. 

For some of them are stronger in the spaces where they are seen and are larger, while others are smaller and thinner; these cannot be seen everywhere at all, and we recognize them only through sight or touch. From this, many are led to believe that these are not bodies, and even that they are merely **places** <note>original: *locos*; the text argues against the idea of "empty space," suggesting that what we perceive as a void is actually filled with subtle bodies</note>, which is impossible. For even without what is said—because the world (if it is indeed a thing) exists in God himself—if it is full of Him and of the **intelligible world** <note>original: *intelligibilium mundum*; the realm of divine forms and pure spirit</note>, that is, similar to His own divinity, then this world which is called **sensible** <note>original: *sensibilis*; the world perceived by the physical senses</note> is also very full of bodies, even though some have argued it was not. We see the forms of all these, whether they are exceedingly large, or some are very short, or nearby...

<summary>Hermes instructs his disciples on the distinction between the higher intellect and physical sense, emphasizing that the universe is a "plenum" filled with bodies, both visible and invisible.</summary>

Concerning Place <note>original: *de loco*</note>

This is what is best demonstrated by measure alone: things outside of the corporeal. Nor can something be measured by the corporeal—that is, what can be discerned by quantity, by the reason of quantity, and by number. For in the divine itself, no such physical quantity consists. Therefore, if this is called the **sensible world** <term>mundus sensibilis: the physical universe perceived by the five senses</term>: it surpasses every quality of sensible things or bodies by its eternal nature. All things can be known by returning them to His dominion. For all things are "gods" <note>Hermetic philosophy often views the stars, planets, and elements as "divine" beings or "gods" within the Great God</note>, and have arisen from Him, and have arisen by His will. 

This whole is good, divine, wise, and immutable: and He alone is both the sensible and the intelligible. And according to **Horus** <note>original: *Hor.*; likely referring to the Egyptian deity Horus, who appears in some Hermetic dialogues as a teacher or archetype of time</note>, there never was anything, nor is now, nor shall be outside of Him. For all things are from Him, and in Him, and through Him; and the gods are treated in multiform ways, in great quantity, and in every measure.

### Apuleius on the Doctrine of Plato

Plato’s physical build gave him his nickname <note>original: *Platoni habudo corpore cognomentu' dedit*; "Plato" comes from the Greek word *platys*, meaning "broad," referring either to his shoulders or his broad forehead</note>. For he was first known as Aristocles: and he was said to be the son of Ariston. On his mother Perictione's side, she was the famous daughter of Glaucus <note>original: *maris*; possibly a transcription error for *Glauci*</note>. And on both sides, his nobility was great. For Ariston <margin>P. Ariston</margin> <note>P. likely stands for *Pater* (Father)</note> traced his origin from Codrus <note>original: *coctum*; likely a corruption of *Codrum*, the last legendary King of Athens</note>, and thus from Neptune himself. From Solon, the wisest man and the giver of laws, Perictione drew this strength and confidence of divine blood.

As many say, speaking with a more restricted understanding: that Apollo joined himself to Perictione in a divine encounter. He was born in the month which among the Athenians is called Thargelion <note>The 11th month of the Attic calendar, roughly May/June</note>, on the day when, at Delos, Latona is said to have given birth to Apollo and Diana. Moreover, some believe he was born the day before. 

There was also a dream involving the poet's birth. For Socrates seemed to himself to have seen a swan chick fly to another altar which is in the Academy, dedicated for a sacrifice to Cupid; and when it had settled in his lap, it afterwards secretly sought the sky with its wings, and its musical song was heard to soothe both men and gods. And when Socrates recounted this on that day in an assembly of men, the beloved boy Plato was presented to him, and Socrates was provided to the master as the suitable student. When he saw him, he looked at the boy's character—both the greatest and the least of it—and said: "This, friends, was the swan from the Cupid of the Academy."

Such a man was Plato, and from such beginnings. He did not only excel in the virtues of heroes, but even aspired to the powers of the gods. For Speusippus <note>Plato's nephew and successor as head of the Academy</note>, instructed by family records, in training youthful minds, praises him as a noble and admirable model for those to come; he records the beauty of his early years, as he was striving with labor and love. He also mentions how great were the proofs of his virtues, and how he was led by them through his progress. Among these same people, Glaucon and Adeimantus were his brothers. He had as his teacher in his first school of letters Dionysius, but in the wrestling-school <term>palaestra</term> <note>original: *paelestra*; a Greek-style wrestling school or gymnasium</note>, he had Ariston.

<summary>This page introduces the life and divine lineage of the philosopher Plato, detailing his noble ancestry, the legend of his birth associated with Apollo, and Socrates' prophetic dream of a swan.</summary>

And after he lost Socrates <note>original: *relist*; likely a corruption of *reliquit* or *amisit* (left or lost)</note>, he sought where he might further profit and betook himself to the discipline of Pythagoras. Although he saw this school provided with such diligent and magnificent instruction, he nonetheless desired even more to imitate the contemplation and purity of their way of life. 

And because the governance of the Pythagoreans provided access to other disciplines, he hastened to Cyrene <note>A Greek city in modern-day Libya</note> to learn geometry, and applied himself to astrology. He sought out Egypt so that he might also learn the rites of the prophets. And he came truly to Italy, and followed the Pythagoreans Archytas of Tarentum and the followers of Echecrates <note>original: *Simoneos acolpna*; likely referring to the Pythagorean community</note>. He would have extended his curiosity even to the Indians and the Magi <margin>or they had sent back</margin> had the Chaldean wars <note>original: *bella caldaica*; likely referring to regional conflicts in the East preventing travel to Persia</note> not broken out at that time. 

Therefore, having traversed these subjects in his youth, and having more studiously prepared himself with the teachings of Zeno, he departed and filled his books with such individual points of admiration that he was the first to join together a **tripartite philosophy** <term>tripartite philosophy</term> <note>The division of philosophy into three branches: Physics (Natural), Ethics (Moral), and Logic (Rational)</note>. He showed that these parts are not disparate or conflicting among themselves, but rather help one another with mutual aid. For although we divide them into specific duties...

### Plato's First Principles

Plato judged that there are three principles of all things: God, and Matter, and the Forms <note>original: *formas*; the eternal, abstract blueprints of reality</note>, which he also calls Ideas <note>original: *ideas*</note>. For since unformed things are dissolved, they are distinguished by no hope of significance among those things that are gathered; if this is also proposed concerning the perception of the senses. We deem this, however, to be immortal. Both are removed from all... and they lack... opinion, needing nothing, he himself unchanging toward the end... which now you may place as something individual, improbable, and as he himself says...

According to him <note>Plato</note>, there are two parts to this art of rhetoric. **Philosophy** ought to be, if it is to be worthy in its character, an effort that is superior in every way, without which men believe that hardships are impossible to tolerate. One should desire nothing so much as to always strive to separate the soul from the body’s temperament. Therefore, philosophy must be confirmed as the meditation and the **practice of dying** <note>original: *meditationem consuetudinemque moriendi*; a classic Platonic and Stoic definition suggesting that the philosopher spends their life detaching the soul from bodily distractions to prepare for its ultimate liberation</note>. It behooves all good men to have friendship among themselves; and if they are less so, there is no path except that which is established through death and the union for the sake of self-love. Pure things do not shrink from their likes. Hence it is established that faithful friendship exists only among the good. 

Wisdom makes one a lover of the good, whereas the fortitude of the body bestows nothing specific on any individual. For when the soul itself is pleased, a man would love the whole, even though the body is the worst part of him. Listen to this: he must be thought [to be wise], or else, if he is ignorant, he may be guarded by the desire for good things. But that indeed is characteristic of the ignorant: is everything the mind sees scarcely certain, just as it is not [real]? Nor is it for that reason that he is loved here for his strength, since the wise man [acts] with a pure will...

<summary>The text argues that true strength is found in the soul rather than the body and defines philosophy as the practice of detaching the soul from physical desires in preparation for death. There are **four types of faulty citizens** <note>original: *Quatuor culpabiliu[m] civiu[m] genera*; this corresponds to Plato’s four stages of political degeneration: Timocracy (honor-driven), Oligarchy (wealth-driven), Democracy (liberty-driven), and Tyranny</note>:
The first is that which seeks to enjoy its own honor.
The second is that of the few.
The third is that of all people.
The last, finally, is **tyranny** <note>original: *tyrannis*</note>.

The first type is seen to follow when, through the office of a magistrate, a more prudent man drives out the seditious. They are deprived of what belongs to them because they are in the hands of the fortunate. For if they act with a more flattering counsel where they can, they obtain that power for themselves if they utilize the violence of the crowd.

The penultimate state, however, shares a nature with those who are perhaps criminal; the wealth of the few is wickedly seized by those who have promised to receive it. In this state, they are not moved by a skill for ruling if there is wealth. This **Popular State** <term>status Popularis: Democracy, or a government by the common people</term> grows strong when the multitude, acting against the power of the wealthy, passes laws so that the will of the people may be promulgated, allowing every citizen to seize honor for himself.

And finally, that singular **tyranny** <note>original: *tyrannis*; here described as "draconian" or absolute rule</note> is the head of all things when one individual obtains his own command in the city. Although he may lead those he has seized into judgment with any form of coercion, he subsequently appears moderate when, following a change, he receives the obedience and prayers of the poor.

# THE ATHENIAN PHILOSOPHER PLATO'S DISCUSSION WITH GORGIAS ON THE ART OF SPEAKING
## In which are introduced Callicles, Socrates, Chaerephon, Polus, and Gorgias.
->Callicles!<-

**Callicles:** In war and battle, O Socrates, it is proper to be a participant in such a way <note>original: *Belli et pugne oportum... ita participem esse*; this is a playful jab at Socrates for arriving just as the performance has ended—much like a soldier arriving at the end of a fight</note>.

**Socrates:** Is it as the saying goes: have we come after the feast? Are we late?

**Callicles:** And indeed, it was a fine feast! For Gorgias has shown us many and excellent things.

**Socrates:** Isn't it so? But, O Callicles, the cause of this is Chaerephon here, who forced us to linger in the marketplace <term>forum: the public square and marketplace where political and social life took place</term>.

**Chaerephon:** It is nothing, Socrates; let that be no hindrance. For I myself will make amends, since Gorgias is my friend. Therefore, whether you prefer it now or at another time, he will show these same things to us.

**Callicles:** What, O Chaerephon? Does Socrates desire to hear Gorgias?

**Chaerephon:** For this very reason we are here. Wherever it pleases you all, let us go to my house. For Gorgias is staying with me, and he will show us his skill.

**Socrates:** Quite right, O Callicles—provided he is willing to answer us if we question him now. For I desire to learn from him just what the power of his art is, and what it is he professes to teach and instruct <note>original: *precipiatq[ue] et doceat*</note>. As for the other matters (as you say), he can show us at another time.

**Callicles:** The best thing, Socrates, is to ask him about this. For that was exactly what he was saying just now. He ordered that everyone present should ask whatever they wished, and he promised he would answer everything.

**Socrates:** Oh, how excellently you tell it! O Chaerephon, ask him yourself.

**Chaerephon:** What shall I ask?

**Socrates:** What he himself is.

**Chaerephon:** How do you mean?

**Socrates:** Just as if he were a maker of shoes and answered—would he not understand himself to be a shoemaker? <note>Socrates frequently uses analogies of humble crafts (like shoemaking or medicine) to define what a true "art" or "science" is.</note>

**Chaerephon:** I understand him, and I will ask him now. Tell me, O Gorgias: is it true what Callicles says, that you have offered to answer all things? Did I then do thus? Do you know how we shall respond?

**Gorgias:** It is true, O Chaerephon. For in what has just passed—and I say nothing new—for many years now no one has asked me anything that I have not already promised to answer.

**Chaerephon:** Is it then so easy, <unclear>ind.</unclear> Gorgias?

<summary>This page contains the opening of Plato's Gorgias, where Socrates and Chaerephon arrive late to an oratory demonstration and prepare to question Gorgias about the nature of his profession.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Gorgias, Rhetoric, Oratory, Dialogue, Chaerephon, Callicles, Athenian Philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the opening scene of Plato's *Gorgias*. Following Socrates’ arrival, the dialogue moves from social pleasantries to a formal inquiry. Socrates’ companion, Chaerephon, begins the questioning, but is intercepted by Polus, a young and eager student of Gorgias. This section highlights the tension between "rhetoric" (beautiful but vague speech) and "dialectic" (precise questioning), which is a central theme of the work.</meta>

**Polus:** Set this aside and ask, O Chaerephon; and you, ask even more faithfully. For it seems that Gorgias is already exhausted <note>original: *iam defessum*; Gorgias had just finished giving a long public exhibition of his speaking skills before Socrates arrived</note>.

**Chaerephon:** What? Do you think, Polus, that you will answer better than Gorgias?

**Polus:** What does it matter to you, provided it is done well?

**Chaerephon:** It matters nothing. What if I ask from here?

**Polus:** Ask.

**Chaerephon:** I am asking then. If Gorgias possesses an art of this kind, such as that which his brother Herodicus possesses, what should we call him? Would we call him the same as his brother?

**Polus:** Yes.

**Chaerephon:** Then we would rightly call him a physician?

**Polus:** Exactly.

**Chaerephon:** And if he were skilled in the same way as Aristophon, the son of Aglaophon, what would we call him?

**Polus:** A painter, obviously.

**Chaerephon:** But now, since Gorgias has skill in another art, what should we say that we call him?

**Polus:** O Chaerephon, many arts have been skillfully discovered among men through experience <term>peritia: knowledge gained through practice rather than theory</term>. For experience causes our life to proceed by art, while inexperience <term>inscitia: ignorance or lack of professional skill</term> causes it to proceed by chance. Different men partake in different arts in different ways—the best men taking part in the best. Among these men is Gorgias here, who is held to possess the best of all arts.

**Socrates:** Indeed, O Gorgias, Polus seems to be well-prepared for speaking; but he has not performed what Chaerephon promised.

**Gorgias:** Why not, O Socrates?

**Socrates:** Because he does not seem to me to have answered the question asked in the slightest.

**Gorgias:** Well, if you wish, you may question him yourself.

**Socrates:** If Gorgias would prefer to answer, I would more gladly ask it of him than of Polus. For it is clear from what Polus just said that he has been more practiced in rhetoric than in dialectic <note>original: *magis in rhetorica quam dialectica*; Socrates is pointing out that Polus gave a flowery "praise" of the art instead of defining what the art actually is</note>.

**Gorgias:** Why do you say that, O Socrates?

**Socrates:** Because when Chaerephon asked what art Gorgias possessed, you, Polus, praised his art as if someone were attacking it; but you did not state what the art itself is. Indeed, you have not yet answered the questioner as to what it actually is.

**Gorgias:** So it seems.

**Socrates:** If it is that art which Gorgias teaches—as Chaerephon previously proposed to you—consider if it might be explained, if not so grandly, then at least briefly. And now tell us: in what art is he skilled, and by what name ought we to call Gorgias? Or rather, O Gorgias, you yourself tell us...

<summary>In this opening exchange, Socrates and Chaerephon attempt to define Gorgias’s profession by comparing it to medicine and painting, while Polus fails to give a direct answer, prompting Socrates to distinguish between decorative rhetoric and logical inquiry.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Gorgias, Polus, Chaerephon, rhetoric, dialectic, physician, painter, experience vs chance, definition of art</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the prologue to the main dialectical inquiry of the dialogue. Socrates has just brushed aside Polus, who was attempting to answer on Gorgias's behalf with flowery but empty praise. Now, Socrates addresses Gorgias directly to define the "art" he practices. The text reflects the Latin translation of Plato's Gorgias (specifically 449a–e), likely the popular Renaissance version by Leonardo Bruni.</meta>

...answer what <strike>it is well</strike> <note>The scribe has struck through "ut bene" (it is well), likely correcting a phrasing error to focus on the proper name of the art.</note> he should be called, and the art in which he is skilled.

**Gor.** Rhetoric, O Socrates. 

**So.** Should we then call you a rhetorician?

**Gor.** Certainly, O Socrates, if you wish to call me what I profess to be—as Homer says <note>A reference to the Iliad or Odyssey, where characters are often introduced by their titles or heroic epithets.</note>.

**So.** I do indeed wish it. 

**Gor.** Call me then.

**So.** And what else? Are you able to make others the same?

**Gor.** I certainly profess to do so. And I promise this, not only here but elsewhere. 

**So.** Would you be willing, Gorgias, to proceed as we are now doing—partly by questioning and partly by answering—and leave that long-windedness of words <note>original: *prolixitate verborum*; referring to the long, ornamental speeches favored by sophists</note> which Polus began using for another time? 

**Gor.** What you wish— <margin>or let us speak</margin> do not mistake me. There are some answers, O Socrates, that cannot be made except with long words. But I will try to answer as briefly as possible. For this is also one of the things I claim: that no one can say the same things in fewer words than I. 

**So.** That is just what is needed, O brief Gorgias. Show me this very thing now; reserve the long-windedness for another time. 

**Gor.** I shall do so, such that you will say you have never heard anyone briefer. 

**So.** Come then. You say you have skill in the art of rhetoric, and that you can make others rhetoricians. What is rhetoric itself about? Just as the art of weaving <term>textoria: the craft of the weaver</term> is about the making of clothes. 

**Gor.** Exactly.

**Socrates:** Now you seem to have shown quite clearly, O **Gorgias**, what you consider this art to be.

But now let us first see this: whether the orator is just, and whether the orator stands in the same relation toward the just, the honorable, the shameful, the bad, and the good as he does toward health and the matters handled in other arts. <meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s *Gorgias*. Socrates is moving from his initial dismissal of rhetoric as a mere "knack" to a formal structural analysis. <margin>
Of the soul
</margin>

...Very aptly indeed. Is **Gorgias** alone the discoverer, and of the art? 
**Gorgias.** But how could it be otherwise? Indeed, in his own art, since for each individual his own tongue and <term>rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasive public speaking.</note> is mentioned. **Socrates.** I will try to say, O **Gorgias**, what seems to me to be in both of them; if it is not so, then let this man [Polus] refute me. <margin>
Legislation [Nomothetica]. Justice. These are for the part of the soul. These are for the part of the body: instruction, the ruling body's good. When the greatest good, justice, is not fit, since they look toward what seems good to the political part.
</margin>

**Socrates.** I say such a thing exists for both the body and the soul, which makes it seem as though the body and soul are in good condition when they are nonetheless in a poor state. **Gorgias.** It is so. **Socrates.** Come then, let me show it more clearly if I can. There are two things. I call them two arts. That which concerns the soul I call the "civil art" <note>original: "civilem voco," referring to the Greek *politikē*, the art of managing the city-state.</note>. The one for the body I cannot name with a single term. However, if I speak of the two parts of the body, I mean gymnastics and medicine. In the civil art, as we said: gymnastics corresponds to <term>legislation</term> <note>original: "nomothetice," from the Greek for the art of making laws.</note>, and medicine corresponds to <term>justice</term>. Yet medicine and gymnastics mix and communicate with each other, just as justice and legislation do, because they both deal with the same thing; nevertheless, they differ from one another. Since these are four, and they always strive for the good of the body or the soul with great effort, <term>flattery</term> <note>original: "adulatio," translating the Greek *kolakeia*, a deceptive imitation of a true art.</note>, knowing this—not by knowledge, but by guesswork—divides itself into four parts. It creeps in under each of these arts and pretends to be that which it has replaced. It has no concern for the actual good, but <term>pleasure</term> always hunts for what is most sweet to soothe the mind, truly through deception, so that it is regarded as being of the greatest value. Thus, <term>cookery</term> <note>original: "coquaria," the art of food preparation.</note> creeps in under medicine, and pretends to know the best foods for the body...

<margin>
and publicly
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Socrates's critique of rhetoric in Plato’s Gorgias. Having established that there are true arts for the body and soul, he now defines "flattery"—the counterfeit practices that mimic those arts to provide pleasure rather than health.</meta>

...I know. Therefore, if it were necessary for these matters to be judged, and let us say all people were involved—just as children, so too those who are ignorant and unskilled <note>original: "aquei," likely a transcription error for "aeque" (equally) or a term for the unlearned.</note>: who among them would understand more about these same good and bad things? Even a child would know the doctor's judgment. 

I call this "flattery," and I tell others, O **Polus**, that it is a base thing, because it concerns itself with pleasure without any rational account <note>original: "rōne" (ratione). Socrates argues that a true art must be able to explain the "why" behind its actions.</note> of what is actually good. I do not call it an art, but rather a certain knack <note>original: "peritiā," translating the Greek *empeiria* (experience/routine).</note>, because it possesses no rational understanding of the nature of the things it offers. Nor could it provide a natural cause or reason for them. For I do not call that an "art" which is performed without reason. 

And if you doubt these things, I am willing to give you a full account in speech. Just as I have described, flattery has crept in under the guise of the doctor <note>This refers to the art of cookery imitating medicine.</note>. In the same way, the dishonest, deceptive, ignoble, and illiberal art of beautification <note>original: "fōreū," likely referring to *fucorum* or the use of dyes and cosmetics.</note> mimics gymnastics. It deceives through shapes, colors, smoothing of the skin, and clothing; it makes people pursue a false beauty that is not their own, while neglecting the proper and true beauty that comes from gymnastics.

So that I might not be too long, I want to speak to you as the geometers <note>Socrates often uses mathematical ratios to explain philosophical relationships.</note> are accustomed to do. For beautification is related to gymnastics just as <term>sophistry</term> <note>The practice of teaching clever but often fallacious arguments for profit.</note> is related to legislation; and what cookery is to medicine, <term>rhetoric</term> <note>The art of persuasion, which Socrates here considers a mere counterfeit of justice.</note> is to justice. This is what I suspect. 

On the other hand, although these things are separate by nature, they are mixed together in practice; and because they deal with the same subjects, sophists and rhetoricians are confused with one another. They do not know their own worthlessness, nor do other men. For if the soul did not command the body—if the soul did not judge for itself, but things were judged by the body—if cookery and medicine were judged by the body itself according to its own labor and pleasure—then that saying of **Anaxagoras** <note>A philosopher who famously claimed that "in the beginning, all things were together."</note> would be most true, O **Polus** (for you are skilled in these matters): all things would be mixed together in the same mass, resulting in a confusion of healthy things, or of nature and cookery. You have heard, then, what I say rhetoric is.

<summary>Socrates argues that tyrants and orators lack true power because they act on whims without wisdom, distinguishing between doing "what seems best" and doing "what one truly wants" (the Good). He begins an analogy comparing painful actions, like taking medicine, to the pursuit of a higher goal like health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s Gorgias, where Socrates and Polus are investigating the difference between doing "what one sees fit" and doing "what one wants." ...to want or to be powerful for the sake of something. **Socrates.** Therefore, does the man who is sailing want this—the sailing itself—or rather that other end for the sake of which he sails? For he does not merely act without a cause: he wants the goal of what he does.
For whoever wants to sail undergoes dangers and endures hardships. It was for the sake of something else that he sailed. It is established that I should admit this.

**Polus.** Nothing else, I admit. **Socrates.** Are not **wisdom**, **health**, **riches**, and other such things "good," and their opposites "bad"? **Polus.** Entirely so. **Socrates.** And those things which are neither good 
nor bad? Those which sometimes share in the good, sometimes in the bad, and sometimes in neither? Such as sitting, walking, running, sailing. 
<note>The word "navigare" is repeated at the end of the previous line and the start of this one.</note>
Sailing. And again, like stones and wood and such things: would you not say these are neither good nor bad? **Polus.** 
Entirely so; **Socrates.** Therefore, do men perform these **neutral** things for the sake of the good, or do they want the good things for the sake of the neutral? 
**Polus.** I admit <note>original: "fa."; shorthand for "fateor," meaning "I confess" or "I admit."</note> they do these neutral things for the sake of the good. **Socrates.** Is it for the sake of the good, then, that 
we walk when we walk? And on the contrary, that we stand when we stand? And is it for the sake of this same good if we kill someone, or expel 
them, or despoil them of their fortune? Do we not think it is better for these things to be done [for some benefit]? 
**Polus.** Surely. **Socrates.** For the sake of the good, then, they do all these things that they do. **Polus.** 
I confess it. **Socrates.** Did we not just agree that when we do something for the sake of another thing, 
we do not "want" those actions, but that for the sake of which we act? **Polus.** That is so. 
**Socrates.** Therefore, we do not simply want to kill, or to expel, or to take away money—
as you just admitted. For those things which are neither 
good nor bad: we do not want them for themselves. Nor do we want things that are bad... 
as we have already seen. Why do you not answer? **Polus.** It seems so <note>original: "vnti"; likely shorthand for "videtur," meaning "it seems so."</note>.

<summary>Socrates argues that people do not "want" the specific actions they perform (like sailing or punishment), but rather the "good" goal they hope to achieve through those actions. <meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s Gorgias. In the preceding text, Socrates argued that men do not truly want the intermediate actions they perform (like sailing or taking medicine), but rather the ultimate "good" they hope to achieve through those actions. **Socrates.** Therefore, if someone does something? If he kills someone or drives them out <note>original: "pellat"</note> or takes away their money, he would prefer this for himself and thinks he is doing what is in his own interest.

**Polus.** As if you, O Socrates, would not choose to have the license to do what you see fit when you see the chance! Nor are you envious of such a man when you see some who have killed, put to death, destroyed, or bound in chains as much as they saw fit?
**Socrates.** Do you mean "justly" or "unjustly"?
**Polus.** Whichever way, both are to be wished for.
**Socrates.** Heaven forbid, O Polus!
**Polus.** Why?
**Socrates.** Because one ought not to wish for something pitiable, nor for a miserable man <note>original: "miserabile vinu[m]"; likely a scribal error where "vinum" (wine) was written instead of "virum" (man).</note>. What did he truly do regarding those of whom I speak?
**Polus.** What do you mean?
**Socrates.** Does he who kills someone whom he thinks it "just" to kill seem miserable to you?
**Polus.** Not exactly; but [the act] is not to be wished for in the same way.
**Socrates.** Did you not say a little while ago, my friend, that the man who does what he sees fit—even if it is just—is the most pitiable and miserable of all? But to him who kills justly, as it seems fit, it is not to be wished for.
**Polus.** But he says that he who kills justly is not pitiable in himself.
**Socrates.** Not at all—even if he is the one who kills, O Polus. And never is he who kills justly miserable.
**Polus.** Then when, O Socrates, is he?
**Socrates.** Because the greatest of all evils is to **do wrong** <term>iniuriam facere: to commit an act of injustice against another</term>.
**Polus.** How so? Is it not a greater evil to **suffer wrong**? <note>original: "iniuria[m] pati"</note>
**Socrates.** Not at all.
**Socrates.** Indeed, I would very much like it if you perhaps...

...all other things, by way of shape and color, or by either the delight or the utility they provide—is this why you call them **beautiful** <note>original: "pulchra"; often translated as "noble" or "fine" in a moral and aesthetic sense</note>? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** And do you view lives and music in the same way? **Polus:** Exactly. **Socrates:** And what of laws and all social practices? Are they not beautiful for any other reason than that they are either useful, or pleasant, or both? **Polus:** So it seems. **Socrates:** And is the beauty of the **sciences** <note>original: "disciplinarum"; referring to branches of learning or organized knowledge</note> the same way? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** You are doing very well now by setting this down, since you define the beautiful by pleasure and utility. **Socrates:** And should not the **shameful** <note>original: "turpe"; the opposite of beautiful, implying moral baseness or ugliness</note> be defined by the opposite: by **pain** <note>original: "molestia"</note> and **harm** <note>original: "detrimento"</note>? **Polus:** That is so. **Socrates:** Therefore, when one of two beautiful things is chosen, and it surpasses the other in beauty, it is because it excels in pleasure, in utility, or in both? **Polus:** Certainly. **Socrates:** And when one of two shameful things is more so than the other, must it not be because it surpasses it in either pain or harm? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** Come then, regarding what was said about **injustice** <note>original: "iurijs" for "injuriis"</note>, whether in the doing or the suffering of it: did we not already assume that doing it is worse? You said doing it is more shameful. If it is more shameful, then must it not exceed in either pain or harm individually, or in both? **Polus:** That is so. **Socrates:** Consider then: does the pain exceed more for those who commit the injustice? **Polus:** It does not seem so. **Socrates:** But if it is not pain, and it does not surpass in both, does it not follow that it surpasses in the other—namely, harm? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** Therefore, doing injustice is called shameful because it surpasses in harm? **Polus:** That is manifest. **Socrates:** And was it not agreed by you and many others a little while ago that doing injustice is more shameful than suffering it? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** And does it not also appear **worse** <note>original: "deterius"</note>? **Polus:** It seems so. **Socrates:** [Fragmented text] ...therefore it is not possible [to choose] the greater rather than the worse and the more shameful... <summary>Socrates leads Polus to define the "Beautiful" as that which provides pleasure or utility, and the "Shameful" as that which causes pain or harm. They conclude that since doing injustice is "more shameful" but not "more painful" than suffering it, it must be "more harmful" and therefore worse.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Latin translation of Plato’s dialogue, the *Gorgias*, specifically the section where Socrates and Polus discuss the moral benefits of punishment. Is **paying the penalty** <note>original: "penas dare"; a Latin idiom for being punished</note> one of these things [undergone by a patient] or not? **Polus:** It is manifest, O Socrates. **Socrates:** Therefore it seems, Polus, to be an action of another. For in this way he understands that he punishes the **worst** <note>original: "pessimum"; referring to the most evil part of himself</note> in himself. **Polus:** That is common. **Socrates:** Is he who pays the penalty freed from a **vice** <note>original: "vitio"; a defect, moral flaw, or disease of the soul</note>? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** Therefore he is freed from the greatest evil. Are their vices not poverty, disease, and **injustice** <note>original: "iniuriam"</note>? **Polus:** Yes. **Socrates:** Which of these is the most **shameful** <note>original: "turpissimum"; the most foul or disgraceful</note>? <summary>Socrates leads Polus to admit that punishment is beneficial because it frees the soul from injustice, which is the most shameful and harmful of all "vices," just as medicine frees the body from disease.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates (abbreviated in this manuscript as "Sol." for *Solutio* or the "Teacher") and a respondent (abbreviated as "Bo." for Boethius, though representing Polus from Plato's *Gorgias*). They are comparing the three types of human "evils"—poverty, disease, and injustice—and determining which is the most detrimental to human happiness.</meta>

In justice, it is more tempered and more healthy: than **poverty** or **disease**. 

**Socrates:** Nor does it seem to be by fortune. 

**Respondent:** Since there is a confusion of clarity and great detriment and a wonderful superiority over vanity: it is the most shameful whenever it is not resolved. 

**Respondent:** But to what is poverty the greatest detriment? 

**Socrates:** It is the greatest of all. In injustice, because it is in the soul, there is the greatest liberation of the soul from the greatest heap of evils. 

**Socrates:** Which [art] liberates us from poverty? 

**Respondent:** Money-making <note>original: "qpusa" / "capusa," likely referring to *chrematistike*, the art of wealth acquisition</note>. 

**Socrates:** Yes. 

**Respondent:** And which from disease? 

**Socrates:** Medicine. 

**Respondent:** What then regarding wickedness and vice? If one falls into them, where and to whom are they led, just as those sick in their bodies are led? 

**Socrates:** They are offered to doctors. 

**Respondent:** Where then do they lead the unjust? 

**Socrates:** To the judge, so that he may be saved through punishment. 

**Respondent:** Yes. 

**Socrates:** In what way is justice carried out to punish them? Or by what reason are they punished? 

**Socrates:** Entirely so. 

**Respondent:** Therefore, money-making frees us from poverty; medicine from disease; and judicial <term>justice</term> <note>original: "iudiciaria"; referring to the corrective power of the legal system</note> frees us from injustice and excess. 

**Socrates:** So it seems. 

**Respondent:** At what point is this most precious thing to be done? 

**Socrates:** It is said. 

**Respondent:** It is necessary for medicine and judicial justice to be performed. 

**Socrates:** By much fortune is it done through the judiciary. 

**Respondent:** Therefore, must the greatest of delights be found in what is base? For each is most excellent if it is thus. 

**Socrates:** Yes. 

**Respondent:** In this way, do those who are cured by medicine delight in it, as those who are cured of poverty rejoice? 

**Socrates:** It does not seem so. 

**Respondent:** But it is truly life-giving, for it liberates from a great evil. 

**Socrates:** Yes, it is not a base thing to tolerate pain so that one may become healthy. 

**Respondent:** In what way is he who (as you say of the body) comes to be healthy? Is it he who is cured by medicine <note>original: "amara utrique"; meaning the treatment is "bitter to both" the doctor and patient</note>, or he who was never sick at all? 

**Socrates:** Clearly, the one who never knew the disease.

<summary>This page explores the Platonic argument that justice/punishment is the "medicine of the soul." It compares poverty, disease, and injustice, concluding that while medical treatment is painful, it is better than remaining sick, just as punishment is better than remaining unjust.</summary>
